title: Ten Most Important Packers for Showdown vs. Bears: He Can’t Be Punching Bag
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers will host the Chicago Bears on Sunday in what could be dubbed a revenge game. The Bears ended the Packers’ hopes at both an NFC North championship and a Super Bowl title a season ago.
After each game, Ben Johnson gave Matt LaFleur a blow-by handshake, and then loudly exclaimed expletives toward the Packers in a video that made its rounds on social media.
Nine months later, the adversaries will face off again. Forget all those storylines, though, the Packers need a win.
The Bears are coming to Lambeau Field, where they have not won a game the Packers’ starting quarterback has finished since 2015. The Bears are playing a backup quarterback, with Tyson Bagent expected to start for injured Caleb Williams.
Allowing the Bears, who are 3-1, to come into Green Bay and drop the Packers to 2-3 could be catastrophic.
Here are the top 10 players to ensure that does not happen.
Teams that like to run the football first have a certain personality. Chicago’s run game took a big hit on Friday when Kyle Monangai was ruled out with a toe injury that has him in a walking boot. Monangai is the running back that gives Chicago’s run game its personality. He’s a violent runner. He runs through people, not around them.
Zaire Franklin is the counter to that personality on defense. He gives the Packers a physical presence in the middle of their defense at linebacker. Even without Monangai, stopping the run is just as much about attitude as it is about ability.
Franklin is also the single biggest replacement for Edgerrin Cooper’s playmaking in the middle of Green Bay’s defense. To be clear, Franklin is not going to replace Cooper. Unless Fred Warner is walking through the door, perhaps that cannot be done at all.
He still needs to be part of the solution.
“It’s great,” linebacker Isaiah McDuffie said about working with Franklin. “He brings it every day. He’s the same guy every day. He’s a great player. He’s a great leader. It’s definitely fun having him in the room, it’s going to be fun being out there with him.”
Chicago’s run game thrives on running outside zone. According to Sharp Stats, Chicago runs outside zone 60 percent of the time on carries given to its running backs.
Green Bay ranks 31st in the NFL against that style of run, giving up 6.2 yards per carry. The Falcons, who rank second in outside zone rate, ran all over the Packers two weeks ago. No, the Bears do not have the individual excellent of Bijan Robinson in their backfield, but they lead the league in rushing yards per game.
Franklin needs to help the Packers remain competitive against Chicago’s run game to force Tyson Bagent to beat them.
“I think it really starts with stopping the run personally,” Franklin said. “No matter how talented of a play-caller you are or how complicated or analytical we get with this football game, football is just run the ball, stop the run, take the ball away. I think if you want to stop any offense you just have to stop the run”
If it can’t do that, it will be a long day for Green Bay’s defense.
Matthew Golden was shut out of the end zone during the regular season as a rookie. His first touchdown came on an impressive catch-and-run against Chicago in the playoffs that reminded everyone of the talent the Packers saw when they made him a first-round pick.
Now, Golden is fully immersed in Green Bay’s offense. He leads the team in targets and often looks like the man that Jordan Love is targeting on the biggest plays of the game.
That dates to last year, as well. With the Packers facing a fourth down and their season on the line, Golden was the target. He converted, but the Packers’ final drive ultimately fell short.
These games are often about the best players making big plays. Golden is capable of that. Chicago’s defense has had some success early in the season against opposing the pass but did struggle with Green Bay’s speed a season ago. Golden is faster than Romeo Doubs, who started all three games Green Bay played against Chicago last year.
Could he be in line for some big plays against a new-look Bears defense?
“I think the main thing is they got some new players out there,” Jordan Love said. “Especially with both safeties being new guys, some of the linebackers being new. The personnel is the main thing that stands out. I think they got a really good defense. They’ve got a great coordinator over there. I’ve got a lot of respect for him and some of the stuff they do.”
New players or not, the best players need to make plays against this defense, which is what Golden is growing into.
Speaking of best players and making plays. Tucker Kraft has certainly not played up to the standard he set a season ago, when it looked like he was going to be in contention for an All-Pro selection.
If Zaire Franklin gives the Packers a personality on defense, it’s Tucker Kraft who gives the Packers their personality on offense in the absence of Josh Jacobs. When Kraft is at his best, he’s punishing defenders by running through them instead of around them.
With all the fanfare surrounding the trash talk on both sides, Kraft kept it simple.
“I talk with my pads,” Kraft said.
In order for Kraft to talk with his pads, however, he needs to catch the ball. Kraft has had a few uncharacteristic drops this season, which have limited his playmaking opportunities.
“I’ve owned it. I dropped the football,” Kraft said. “I think I’m just trying to do too much. Offensively, we might get into a lull and I think I can make the game-saving play right there. I’m taking my eyes off the ball. Can’t do anything without the ball, so I’m just going to slow down and play my role, catch the football.”
Sunday’s game is the style of game that the Packers need to play clean. Chicago is the best team in the league in possessing the football, which means more mistakes by Green Bay’s offense, means more time on the field for their defense. Drops, fumbles and penalties are killer.
They hurt even more when it’s a team captain making a mental mistake. Those types of mistakes cannot happen against a team that the Packers are chasing in the division.
In the absence of Edgerrin Cooper, the Packers are searching for playmakers on defense. Last week, that was safety Evan Williams, who is emerging as one of the top players on Green Bay’s defense.
Last year at Lambeau Field, Williams was nearly the goat of Green Bay’s 28-21 win over the Bears. Williams jumped a route, leaving Cole Kmet, his man, unattended in the end zone for what could have been a game-tying touchdown.
As Williams tells it, Keisean Nixon saved him while comparing Nixon to Jesus of Nazareth.
Williams can’t afford to be caught in a position to need a savior this week. For all the fanfare surrounding Chicago’s quarterback position, Tyson Bagent put the ball in harm’s way several times last week against the New York Jets.

If the Packers can get the Bears into obvious passing situations, the ball will have a chance to find the waiting hands of some Packers’ defensive backs.
Williams was the one who picked off Jalon Daniels last week to set up Green Bay’s first touchdown. As the game wound down, it was Williams who Jonathan Gannon called on to close out the Bucs.

Whether it’s as a blitzer or playmaker, Williams needs to be at his best.

title: These Three Critical Factors Are Why Packers Will Lose to Bears … Again
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers used to own the Chicago Bears. When the Bears walk onto Lambeau Field on Sunday for the 214th meeting in the rivalry’s storied history, Ben Johnson will have a pen to sign the deed.
After snapping Green Bay’s 11-game winning streak in the series, the Bears have won three of the last four meetings. Those include, of course, Green Bay’s collapse in December and its epic collapse in the playoffs.
Here are three reasons why the Bears will win again and officially stamp themselves as the team to beat in this new era of the rivalry.
Part 1 of our weekly pair of stories explores 3️⃣ reasons why the Packers will beat the Bears on Sunday. ⬇️ https://t.co/cZq1P0Kxm6
Games are won and lost in the trenches. Everyone knows that – especially after the Packers were blown out in the fourth quarter by the Vikings, barely beat the Jets and were crushed by the Falcons.
Green Bay’s offensive line took a step forward in last week’s escape from Tampa. Jordan Love typically had time to throw the football and the running backs got into the open field a couple times.
While Green Bay’s offensive line has improved, Chicago’s offensive line is an impenetrable force. Look at the teams’ recent games against the Jets for proof.
In Week 2, the Packers rushed the ball 18 times for 63 yards, quarterback Jordan Love was sacked three times and they went 1-of-9 on third down. In Week 4, the Bears rushed for 232 yards, quarterback Tyson Bagent was sacked once and they went 7-of-15 on third down.
In other words, the Jets’ defense handled the Packers but got manhandled by the Bears.
Chicago’s starting left tackle, Braxton Jones, is on injured reserve, but left guard Joe Thuney, right guard Jonah Jackson and center Garrett Bradbury – the pivot in the pivot after Drew Dalman’s retirement – form one of the top interior trios in the league, and Darnell Wright is about as good as it gets at right tackle.
Top running back Kyle Monangai is out with a toe injury, but will it matter with that powerhouse crew opening the holes? Tyson Bagent, obviously, isn’t Caleb Williams, but any competent quarterback can complete passes from a clean pocket.
Personnel decisions have been factors. In 2025, the Packers signed Aaron Banks in free agency in hopes of adding some needed talent and power to the offensive line. That $77 million signing was a disaster, though, with Banks set to be inactive for the fourth time in five games.
The Bears, meanwhile, traded a fourth-round pick to the Chiefs for Thuney and a sixth-round pick to the Rams for Jackson. Those trades were home runs – a big reason why the most dominant unit on the field on Sunday will be Chicago’s line.
The Packers were in control against the Bears in Week 16 but melted down and lost. The Packers were in complete control in the playoff rematch but self-destructed in historic fashion.
With those two games a big part of the equation, the Packers are 2-7 in their last nine games. They no longer look like a team capable of competing for a championship. They are guilty of too many stupid penalties, they drop too many passes, they fumble too often. When push comes to shove, are the Packers capable of doing the pushing?
“I feel like he [coach Ben Johnson] wants to beat them really bad, like everybody else in the room, every Chicago fan,” receiver Luther Burden said. “We just want to beat them real bad and make them quit.”
What a phrase. “Make them quit.”
It’s not all that different from what then-Jets coach Robert Saleh told his team at halftime in a game at Lambeau Field in 2022.
“The mindset to go 60 minutes," said Saleh. "And to give them 60 percent more. And just keep giving them body blow after body blow after body blow. And just keep hitting them, keep hitting them in the mouth. We felt like if we could just keep taking them down to deep water, they’ll find out they can’t swim. It was just a mindset.”
There are questions about the Packers’ talent, especially with tens of millions of dollars sidelined . There are questions, as well, about their mental toughness and ability to weather the storms that undoubtedly will come against top opponents.
Johnson is an X-factor coach. He was as offensive coordinator of the Lions and he is while guiding the Bears’ return from the NFL abyss.
“It’s a really good offense, man,” Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon said. “Ben does an unbelievable job. I think his coaches do an unbelievable job of getting their guys to schematically execute, technically execute plays the right way. They block really well, they run really well, they throw and catch really well, and he puts them in positions to put the defense at a disadvantage. That’s why he is who he is.”
Meanwhile, this is what tight end Tucker Kraft said about LaFleur’s offense: “Defenses know what we’re going to run but we just outexecute their look.”
He didn’t mean that in a derogatory way. It was Kraft answering a question about why he believes the Packers’ offense is close to hitting its stride – that once the execution comes, the points will follow.
Nobody would ever call Johnson’s offense predictable. He’s one of the smartest play-designers and play-callers in the league – and he knows it. He’s brash, yes. And, like any bully, it’ll be interesting to see how he handles getting punched in the mouth.
To be sure, the Packers-Bears rivalry is back because there’s a coaching rivalry, too. Johnson keeps needling LaFleur because he thinks he can get away with it. Until LaFleur’s team rises to the occasion, it’ll be clear which coach has the upper hand.
Last week, Green Bay got its best offensive line performance of the season. The running game showed some life and the pass protection held up.
And yet, the Packers went 2-of-10 on third down – sending the worst third-down attack into the league plunging even further to a ghastly 26.1 percent. Dating to 1972, when the league began tracking third-down data, that’s the 12th-worst of the last 54 seasons. It’s the fifth-worst over the last two decades. The Packers have never finished at worse than 33.7 percent over that period.
Meanwhile, Chicago’s defense is second in the league at 23.7 percent. It just pitched a 0-for-7 shutout against the Jets. Chicago has given up a league-low nine conversions in 33 passing attempts. Green Bay has a league-low 12 third-down conversions through the air.
Jordan Love’s third-down passer rating is a woeful 64.7. A total of 28 quarterbacks have thrown at least 20 passes on third down. Love’s completion rate of 46.3 percent ranks 27th. He is third in third-down attempts but 19th in third-down conversions.
“We talked about the No. 1 factor being the pass game efficiency on both sides of the ball,” Bears coach Ben Johnson said. “To put it in a layman's terms, if our quarterback plays better than your quarterback, we have a good shot of winning the ballgame.
“I felt like the last two weeks, in particular, we really affected the quarterback through both the rush and the coverage aspect of it. Whether we're rushing four or whether we're bringing pressure I think these guys are all working together at a high clip right now.”
Green Bay’s average third down requires 7.9 yards, according to Stathhead. Only four teams are facing a longer distance. That’s one reason why the team has a rather incredible third-down play selection of 42 passes and four runs.
“We got to be better on first and second down, cleaning up penalties, obviously getting positive plays,” Love said. “But that’s the game. You’re always trying to put yourself in third-and-manageable and avoid third-and-longs, and that’s obviously a big part of why our numbers are so bad on third down is we’re in some tough third-down looks.
“But that’s never an excuse. No matter what it is, we got to find a way to go out there and execute and convert some of these third downs. But it definitely starts with cleaning up the penalties and some of the negative plays on first and second down.”

title: Saturday’s Packers Roster Moves: What They Mean for Sunday vs. Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers placed running back Chris Brooks on injured reserve on Saturday. It was the only roster move of the day in advance of Sunday’s home game against the Chicago Bears.
Sometimes, the roster moves that weren’t made are just as interesting as the transactions that were made. Here’s our weekly look.
For the fourth consecutive game, the Packers did not elevate anyone from the practice squad.
That means Mekhi Becton’s Packers debut will have to wait another week.
With left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and right guard Jacob Monk (quad) doubtful and Jager Burton questionable after dealing with back spasms this week, the door seemed to be open for Becton to be added to the gameday roster.
Instead, Green Bay figures to go with Jordan Morgan, Laken Tomlinson, Sean Rhyan, Kevin Zeitler and Anthony Belton as the starters and some combination of Burton, Travis Glover, Donovan Jennings and John Williams as the three or four backups.
The big question will be at right guard. Will the Packers go with Glover, who performed well in his first NFL start last week at Tampa Bay, or Zeitler, the veteran who was signed to bring vital stability to a porous line.
“Feels much better than last week,” Zeitler said on Friday. “Any time you get into a situation like, every rep, every day, just helps more and more, so a lot of improvement over one week.”
Whether he starts or not, Glover has made the team rethink his long-term viability after sitting out last season with a shoulder injury and not really getting a chance to compete for a starting job during training camp this year.
Becton has been working on the right side at guard and tackle. That’s where Glover has been locked in, going all the way back to training camp, when his reps were split between right guard and right tackle.
Glover’s solid performance against the Bucs probably is part of the team’s thinking with Becton, who is getting ramped up after not being with a team during training camp.
“The last couple weeks he had been practicing really well, so Coach Butkus came into my office last week and said ‘Hey, let’s give Glover a shot,’” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich explained on Tuesday. “I thought he did a nice job. He competed hard. There were some plays I’m sure he’d like to get back. He had a penalty but, other than that, played hard, did a nice job in protection. He’s a physical player, so it was good to have him out there, and I’m glad he was able to step up for us.”
This decision isn’t a surprise.
Brooks got the start last week against the Bucs but his day ended in the first half with an ankle injury. On Thursday, the team promoted running back Pierre Strong from the practice squad. Had Brooks been dealing with a week-to-week injury, the Packers could have elevated Strong from the practice squad for a week or two and used the vacant spot for someone else, such as receiver Savion Williams, who returned to practice this week after opening the season on injured reserve.
Instead, Strong will get an extended look with Brooks to be sidelined for at least the next four weeks.
“We’ll leave that with the coaches,” Strong said of his role . “We all good backs. We all great backs. We all can take one to the house any given day. So, I’m just going to leave that to the coaches. Whenever my number’s called, I’m going to be ready.”
Brooks will be a key loss. He’s carried 15 times for 70 yards, highlighted by a 27-yarder last week, and added three receptions for 24 yards. His reliability as a pass protector can’t be replaced by any of the backs on the roster. Plus, he tied for the team lead with 14 tackles on special teams last year.
“I think MarShawn’s done a nice job when he’s been in there. Kaleb obviously will get more opportunities in those situations,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said of MarShawn Lloyd and Kaleb Johnson. “Chris is important, not only in that role but also on special teams and everything that he does for our team. He’s a good leader, hard-nosed guy, so we’ll see where he’s at this week and then see what happens.”
The Bears announced that they activated linebacker Noah Sewell from injured reserve. Two others who had been designated for return and practiced all week, slot Kyler Gordon (calf) and defensive tackle Shemar Turner (knee) were not activated and downgraded to out.
Sewell had a career-high 54 tackles for the Bears last season, when he started nine games. He had one tackle in each of last year’s regular-season games against Green Bay. His role will be to bolster the special teams, which will have to contend with Skyy Moore.
Gordon has played in 45 games with 35 starts in his career. He has five interceptions and 10 tackles for losses. He had two breakups in the Bears’ playoff victory over Green Bay. Turner was a second-round pick last year. He had six tackles, including two TFLs, in five games as a rookie. He did not play in any of the games against Green Bay.
The Bears also elevated running back Zavier Scott from the practice squad. With Kyle Monangai out with a toe injury, he will provide depth behind Sunday’s one-two punch of D’Andre Swift and Roschon Johnson.
Scott entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2023. Last year with the Vikings, he carried 32 times for 114 yards and caught 14 passes for 98 yards.

title: Predicting Three Reasons, Including a Surprise, Why Packers Will Beat Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – For the better part of three decades, the Green Bay Packers beat, bashed and bullied the Chicago Bears. It was the most one-sided rivalry imaginable, a series turned around by Brett Favre and turned into a rout by Aaron Rodgers.
Finally, Packers-Bears means something again. Led by brash coach Ben Johnson, the Bears stunned the Packers twice in the span of four weeks last season. The Bears think they’re big … bleep – and they should think that way.
For the 214th time in series history, these ancient rivals will collide. Sunday’s showdown at Lambeau Field will be huge for Green Bay for a multitude of reasons. For the rivalry. For the standings. For themselves.
Here are three reasons why the Packers will win, with the other side of this story coming on Saturday evening.
The Packers this week didn’t have much to say in response to Bears coach Ben Johnson’s infamous “F*** the Packers” line from after last year’s playoffs or receiver Luther Burden proclaiming this week that the goal was to make the Packers quit.
“We’ll see them boys Sunday,” safety Javon Bullard said in response to Burden’s comment.
Only when it was pointed out the NFL had moved the kickoff from 3:25 p.m. to noon did Bullard break the ice.
“We’re trying to kick their ass. That’s the idea,” Bullard said. “Whether it’s at 7:15, 8:15, 1 o’clock, 3:45, it don’t really matter. We’re playing the Bears. They don’t like us, we don’t like them. It’s going to be primetime for us, regardless.”
The undefeated Vikings lead the NFC North, but the Bears have made an early statement that they are one of the best teams in the league. They’ve won back-to-back games with backup quarterbacks. Their supposedly luck-driven defense from last year is fourth in points allowed. Their third-down defense would make Mike Ditka’s 1985 Bears proud.
The Packers, on the other hand, must be one of the worst 2-2 teams of all-time. There’s nothing they have done at a playoff-caliber level. Moreover, they were humiliated in Week 16 at Chicago and humiliated again in the playoff rematch.
So, when Johnson says, “F*** the Packers,” of course it bothers players like Tucker Kraft.
“Yeah, I guess,” he said. “I talk with my pads, so I’ll just wait ‘til Sunday.”
Really, nothing matters until the Packers beat the Bears. Literally nothing. The Packers have to beat the want-to-be bully Bears, no different than Ralphie had to beat up the bully Scott Farkus in A Christmas Story . They have to do it for the rivalry, for the standings, for their psyche.
The Packers are aware of all of these things. They’ll be ready in their own way for a game that’s important for the Bears but of critical importance for the Packers.
“Yeah, anytime it’s a division game, you kind of got to get your piss hot for the most part, understanding that these are going to have long-term effects on the standings for where we want to be at the end of the year,” safety Evan Williams said.
“And also carrying over from last year, understanding we also have a bad taste in our mouth from what happened. You can understand a 12-round fight. It’s going to be a fistfight for sure. We wouldn’t want anything else.”
Like we wrote last week , sometimes you don’t have to overthink things. The quarterback matchup is Jordan Love against Tyson Bagent.
Last week’s 17-14 win over Tampa Bay won’t be put on Love’s list of personal highlights. But he threw a couple touchdown passes, was given excellent pass protection and largely played mistake-play football until his late-game interception.
Asked about Love on Thursday, Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said:
“Yeah, I see a guy that, if he’s got a clean pocket and he can throw the ball, in rhythm and timing, he’s as good as there is in the league. I think he’s an outstanding quarterback, and I think he’s a tough challenge for us.”
The “clean pocket” part is critical for all quarterbacks and demonstratively true for Love. When pressured, he’s completed 37.0 percent of his passes, averaged 6.1 yards per attempt and thrown zero touchdowns and two interceptions, good for a 43.0 passer rating. When protected, he’s completed 67.0 percent of his passes, averaged 7.1 yards per attempt and thrown eight touchdowns and one interception, good for a 110.0 passer rating.
In last year’s playoff loss to Chicago, Love was under siege during the second-half meltdown. He went 6-of-16 for 71 yards when pressured compared to 18-of-30 for 252 yards from a clean pocket.
With a new offensive line, Love was allowed to play a new game last week. That group could be even better this week with the presumed debut of Kevin Zeitler at right guard.
The Bears, meanwhile, are a middle-of-the-pack 13th in pressure percentage. There’s a chance for Love to have a good day. He’s had a bunch of them against Chicago. As noted by Stats Perform, Love has averaged 9.54 yards per attempt in six career starts against Chicago. That’s the second-highest for any quarterback who’s made at least five starts against an opponent behind only Lamar Jackson’s 10.33 vs. Miami.
And with a backup on the other side of the field, there’s a chance for the Packers’ defense to make a couple game-turning plays, as was the case against Tampa Bay’s Jalon Daniels last week.
There couldn’t possibly be a bigger statistical matchup than the teams’ rushing attacks. Chicago is first in the NFL with 196.3 rushing yards per game while Green Bay is last in the NFL with 58.0 rushing yards per game.
If the Bears enjoy a disparity of about 125 yards on Sunday, they are going to steamroll their way to a Mike Ditka-esque victory. However, a few things could make this a little less of a mismatch.
One, premier running back Kyle Monangai will not play. He entered the week ranked seventh in the NFL in rushing. Of the 38 backs with at least 30 rushing attempts, he’s eighth with 3.75 yards after contact per carry, according to Pro Football Focus. He’s really the driving force behind everything the Bears want to be about offensively.
Two, the Bears will have to lean on D’Andre Swift. Swift is an excellent player, to be sure, with three consecutive seasons of more than 1,250 rushing and receiving yards, but he fumbled twice last week against the Jets.
“We do ball security every single day,” Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor told reporters this week, sounding a lot like Packers coach Matt LaFleur. “We start practice with ball security. We emphasize it. We make a great emphasis to our scout-team defense to make attempts at the ball. …
“The second (fumble) was egregious. That just goes back to our fundamentals, how we expect guys to carry the football. We talk about that every single Saturday. But when guys are out there, that’s the No. 1 point of emphasis on anything we do. We talk about scheme, but we talk about our fundamentals more than anything.”
Three, the Packers’ run game showed a little life last week in Laken Tomlinson’s debut at left guard. Now, Kevin Zeitler might make his debut at right guard. An interior trio of Tomlinson, center Sean Rhyan and Zeitler could be effective not just on Sunday but the long haul.
“We got the job done, man,” Rhyan said on Wednesday. “We were running the ball like we said we wanted to. Protecting like we said we were going to. Everything we said we wanted to do I think we did a pretty good job of doing. Obviously, we got to clean a few things up, but definitely took a step in the right direction.”
Four, Chicago’s run defense is a woeful 28th with 4.94 yards allowed per carry. In its one road game, at Carolina in the opener, the Bears allowed 125 yards on 22 carries, or 5.68 yards allowed per carry. They were 30th in yards allowed per carry in road games last year, too.
Added together, nobody should expect Kaleb Johnson to outrush Swift. But so long as the Packers don’t get run out of Lambeau Field on both sides of the ball, they’ll have a chance to spring the season-changing upset.

title: Hyde and Seek: Without Edgerrin Cooper, Packers Need Evan Williams to Continue Rise
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – In 2024, Bobby Babich had just become the Buffalo Bills’ defensive coordinator. One of the safety prospects in that year’s draft class was Evan Williams.
“I remembered evaling him coming out of college, and I knew he was a dang good player,” Babich, who’s in his first season as Green Bay’s secondary coach and defensive passing game coordinator, told Packers On SI on Friday. “He’s obviously showing the world right now that the Packers made a good choice.”
A fourth-round pick in 2024, Williams has gone from good (all-rookie) to really good (team-high three interceptions in 2025) to bordering on great. With Edgerrin Cooper out with a torn Achilles, Williams did what the best players do by making some pivotal plays in Green Bay’s victory over Tampa Bay.
Williams was a factor deep with one interception and one additional pass breakup. And he was a factor at the line of scrimmage with a sack and quarterback hit on the final series.
That’s an elite safety skill-set.
“As a safety, being one-dimensional is not as sexy as being two-dimensional,” Babich said. “My opinion over my years is that you’ve got to be a threat deep and you’ve got to be a threat at or near the line of scrimmage. And generally, if that’s the case – if you can affect the game both in deep zones and at or near the line of scrimmage – that to me is really what an all-around safety is all about.”
Williams is off to a great start. He might have to find another level to his game without Cooper for the rest of the season.
“You’re losing a guy who’s a tone-setter, a game-changer, just somebody that comes out every game and sets the tone in the run game and in the pass game, is extremely instinctive, is flying all over the field,” Williams said this week. “It’s not easy to replace a guy like that, but I feel like the first thing that comes to my mind is just having trust in everybody.
“It’s a next-man-up type of league. You can’t completely alter your game plan because you have one person out. For the most part, it’s just about trusting that next guy is going to do exactly – I don’t know if you’re going to say exactly what Coop is capable of doing – but just understanding that he’s going to do his job, and being able to play off those guys. It’s all about physicality. We’ve got to show up.”
From defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon’s perspective, adjusting to life without Cooper will be about how much the rest of the defenders can take on without slowing them down mentally.
“That’s always kind of a give-and-take,” Gannon said. “Like, how much is too much, where you’re making them think too much and not just play free and fast? So, I always think, ‘What’s the intent of the call? What’s the strength? What’s the stress?’ As long as they know that and they can get to the technique that they need to use by what their eyes are seeing, then you feel pretty good about doing some of the things that we’re doing.”
Williams has shown he can handle a lot, whether it's a sack against the Bucs or a deep pass breakup at the Jets. It’s why he’s conjured up comparisons to another midround draft pick who wore No. 33 for the Packers.
Hyde was a fifth-round pick in 2013 who had four quality seasons with the Packers. His game hit new heights with Babich and the Bills, including a pair of All-Pro seasons.
“I think with the situation in the fact that they were drafted, where they were drafted, and ba, ba, ba, ba, ba and, obviously, getting drafted by the Packers,” Babich said. “It’s funny, Micah just FaceTimed me two nights ago. But I would say situationally, their games aren’t 100 percent the same, but the way they impact the game is very similar.
“The way that Evan has impacted the game thus far, I would call that similar. I think their games are a little bit different. Every safety that I’ve ever coached is not shaped the same way and their games are all a little bit different, but all the really good ones that I’ve coached – and I’ve been pretty fortunate to coach some good ones – but he’s definitely trending upward he’s got to be consistent with it.”
For the really good safeties – and this was as true for Hyde as Xavier McKinney – the ball just seems to find them. That’s not luck but preparation and instincts combining with talent.
“Usually in the secondary, if you are disciplined during the snap – and I tell the guys this all the time – you don’t know when the ball’s coming to you,” Babich said. “So, the consistency and your discipline within the snap is going to allow you to be in position when that ball shows up. It might not be the 18th time, it might not be the 19th time, but that 20th time that you’ve got that rep, that ball shows up, you just got to be in position to make a play.”
Without Cooper and with Micah Parsons still working his way back, the Packers must find a way on Sunday. The Bears have injury issues, too, and what’s left of the Packers must take advantage to turn the tables on brash Ben Johnson’s rising team.
“It’s hard not to see it,” Williams said of Johnson’s disdain for the Packers. “But, personally, you know, it’s not me. I’m just somebody that doesn’t deal too heavily into the talking. Like, it’s easy to have a camera in front of you and say whatever you want. You know that’s not going to stop you from getting hit in the mouth on any given Sunday.
“And so, to me, it’s always been about the work, about how you show up on Sunday. The talk, it’s fluff to me. And, honestly, I just laugh. Like, ‘OK, you give me a little extra motivation,’ so that you know when I show up and come to pop one of the backs, it’s all right. Now that’s on my mind instead.”
You get what you pay for, as the saying goes. Usually. But not always. The NFL salary cap is $301.2 million. A huge percentage of the Packers' allotment will on the sideline vs. Chicago through, for the most part, no fault of anyone.⬇️ https://t.co/XDjeQj5k1B

title: Here’s Why Pierre Strong Could Secure Critical Role for Packers vs. Bears
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Following Sunday’s victory at Tampa Bay, Green Bay Packers coach Matt LaFleur was irritated for multiple reasons.
At or near the top of the list were two fumbles in a span of four plays by running backs MarShawn Lloyd and Kaleb Johnson. Lloyd’s fumble dribbled out of bounds. Johnson’s fumble at the goal line was recovered by the Buccaneers. Without the fumble, the Packers might have won comfortably; because of the fumble, they barely beat a winless team with an undrafted rookie quarterback making his NFL debut.
“I think a great teacher’s the bench,” LaFleur said after the game. “If guys don’t start holding onto the ball, they’re going to be sitting on the bench.”
For Sunday’s game against the Chicago Bears, Chris Brooks – who started against the Buccaneers – is out with an ankle injury . In his place will be Pierre Strong, who was promoted from the practice squad on Thursday .
Only LaFleur knows the plan for how he’ll handle the backfield on Sunday. Maybe Lloyd and Johnson will carry the load, with Strong in reserve and playing on special teams. That’s typically what would happen with a player pulled up from the practice squad. Heck, that’s what happened with Strong last season. He was elevated three times for gamedays but didn’t play in any of the games.
On the other hand, if LaFleur was truly serious about using the bench as a teacher, maybe Strong will have a key role against the Bears.
Even now, with his season and Packers debut a couple days away, he’s the team’s most accomplished running back. A fourth-round pick by the Patriots in 2022, he played in 46 games from 2022 through 2024 and had a combined 125 rushes and catches. So, this isn’t some rookie. There should be a trust factor based on his play in the preseason.
“Yeah, P’s done a great job ever since he’s gotten here,” LaFleur said on Friday. “He helps on special teams, as well. I think he’s a natural runner. He’s got experience. He’s been in this league a while now, although he has limited I would say game action. If given the opportunity, I think he’ll be ready to go.”
It’s been a long time since Strong played in a game. He carried the ball five times for the Browns in the final game of the 2024 season. He didn’t make their roster in 2025 and landed on Green Bay’s practice squad, where he spent the entire season.
“Man, I could just thank the Lord,” he said after practice. “Like you said, it was a while but God’s timing is better than everybody’s timing. I’m here now so got to continue to get better.”
As the saying goes, you don’t have to get ready if you stay ready. That’s Strong. He was one of the primary ball-carriers throughout training camp and the preseason. He fell short of a roster spot, though, after the Packers traded for Johnson, but he re-signed to the practice squad.
“Yeah, I come to practice every day ready, training like I’m going to play on Sundays because, being on P-squad, you never really know,” he said. “Last year, I got called up sometimes on Saturdays. On P-squad, you’ve always got to be prepared and be ready to work because that’s your job – being prepared.”
As is typically the case, one man’s pain is another man’s gain. He was excited when told on Thursday that he was going to be promoted to the active roster rather than just elevated from the practice squad.
“Man, it was surreal when I got the call,” he said. “We had just got out of practice. I wasn’t expecting anything. Like I said, I come to work every day practicing like I’m going to play on Sundays. Yeah, man, I’m just happy, man. Grateful, but it’s just getting started. Like I got the call, now I got to stay here.”
Strong gave a glimpse of what he can do in the preseason. He’s got excellent vision, a knack for finding cutback lanes and the speed to take advantage. He had a long kickoff return at Denver in the preseason. While he might not be in the running to return kicks on Sunday, he did have 17 tackles in the kicking game in three seasons – the first of which was in New England alongside Packers special teams coordinator Cam Achord.
So, what will bring to the party against Chicago?
“Man, everything a back can do. Passing, blocking, running,” he said. “Whatever play is called I’m going to execute play by play. Just bring everything I can to win this game.”
Green Bay’s running game could use a jolt. It ranks last in the NFL in rushing yards per game and 31st in rushing yards per carry. The team’s leading rusher, Lloyd, is averaging 2.7 yards per carry. Johnson is averaging 4.0 yards per carry but has fumbled twice.
So, nobody has solidified his role, meaning Strong has a golden opportunity to go from the practice squad to a vital part of the offense.
“We’ll leave that with the coaches,” he said. “We all good backs. We all great backs. We all can take one to the house any given day. So, I’m just going to leave that to the coaches. Whenever my number’s called, I’m going to be ready.”
But what if he gets rolling?
“If I get rolling, I’m rolling,” he said.
You get what you pay for, as the saying goes. Usually. But not always. The NFL salary cap is $301.2 million. A huge percentage of the Packers' allotment will on the sideline vs. Chicago through, for the most part, no fault of anyone.⬇️ https://t.co/XDjeQj5k1B

title: Packers-Bears Final Injury Report: Green Bay Gets Season-Changing Opportunities
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – As they muddle through their sputtering start to the season, the Green Bay Packers have been given a two-headed monster of opportunities for Sunday’s game against the so-called Monsters of the Midway, the Chicago Bears.
First, star quarterback Caleb Williams suffered a hamstring injury a few weeks ago. It was interesting, at least, that he returned to practice on Friday and was listed as questionable on the final injury report, but he is expected to be inactive for a third consecutive week. The Packers knew that and have been preparing for backup Tyson Bagent.
Now, the Bears will line up without their best running back, Kyle Monangai. He entered Week 5 ranked seventh in the NFL with 324 rushing yards and sixth with a 5.4-yard average. So, the Packers will have a better chance to stop the pass without Williams and now they will have a better chance to stop the run without Monangai.
Running back Chris Brooks, who started against Tampa Bay last week, is out with an ankle injury. The Packers promoted running back Pierre Strong from the practice squad on Thursday and he’s ready to play in his first game since the 2024 finale for the Browns.
“I always train like I’m ready to play,” he said. “Especially being on P-squad, you never know really when you’re going to be called up, so I always prepare and train like I’m ready to play.”
Savion Williams, who was designated for return from injured reserve this week after missing the start of the season with an ankle injury, is out, as well.
“He’s done well in limited action,” LaFleur said of Williams. “We’re just trying to ramp him up, give him a little bit more each and every day.”
The former starting guards, Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and Jacob Monk (quad), are doubtful. Banks, who played the first half of the Week 2 game against the Jets, did not practice on Wednesday and Thursday but was limited on Friday. Monk, who was injured late in the Week 3 game against Atlanta, returned to practice as limited participation on Friday, as well.
Kevin Zeitler wasn’t about to spill any beans, but he might be ready to make his Packers debut at right guard following last week’s ramp-up. He said he feels “much better” now compared to this time last week.
“Just going to keep attacking 'til game day gets here and we'll see what the best option is for that day,” he said after Friday’s practice.
He said he got “a couple” team reps this week as he learns the offense on the fly.
“Still a lot to process coming in already into season,” he said.
Defensive tackles Javon Hargrave and Anthony Campbell and guard/center Jager Burton are questionable. Hargrave was added to the injury report after being limited on Friday.
When Kyle Monangai didn’t practice on Wednesday, coach Ben Johnson hinted it was more of a rest day after he got 30 carries against the Jets. However, Monangai didn’t practice this week and was in a walking boot at the end of the week.
“We were certainly conscious of the thumb, and it turns out the toe is a bigger deal than we initially anticipated,” he told reporters on Friday morning. “He'll be out this week. He won't be participating in this game, and we'll see how long that injury sidelines him. We got him with a specialist, and we'll work through that.”
So, the Packers, who are 2-2 and dealing with tens of millions of dollars of injuries , will face backup quarterback, Tyson Bagent, along with the running back tandem of D’Andre Swift and Roschon Johnson. It will still be a lightning-and-thunder tandem, with Swift the slasher and Johnson a burly 227 pounds.
Coming off a season of 1,087 rushing yards and three consecutive seasons of more than 1,250 total yards, Swift entered the week ranked eighth with 311 rushing yards, highlighted by 124 yards and three touchdowns in the blowout win over Carolina in Week 1. He’s averaging 4.5 yards per carry but got in the doghouse last week after fumbling twice against the Jets.
Johnson, a fourth-round pick in 2023, had two carries in seven games last season and four carries in seven games this year. He did rush for 352 yards with 34 catches as a rookie and ran for six touchdowns in 2024.
“They’ve got a great duo, one of the best duos in the league,” safety Evan Williams said this week of the Monangai-Swift pairing. “I feel like what they do really well is fall forward. Swift is a probably a little more of a finesse back, but still a guy that can lower his shoulder and deliver a punch when you know when he’s coming through a hole. Monangai, he’s a little less of the finesse and more of your true, downhill-type running back.”
However, three starting linemen who did not practice on Wednesday are ready to go for Sunday.
Three players who the Bears have designated for return from injured reserve, nickel Kyler Gordon, defensive tackle Shemar Turner and linebacker Noah Sewell, were full participation all week and are questionable.

title: Texans Rule Out 7 Players Ahead of Week 5 Titans Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans and Tennessee Titans have revealed their inactives list as their Week 5 matchup sits right around the corner .
And for the Texans, they'll be without a select seven players for this Sunday in Nashville––most of which are pretty predictable absences.
Let's break down what to make of the inactives for both the Texans and Titans as Week 5 is about to get underway:
CB Collin Wright DE Chris Braswell DE Sabastian Harris LB Aiden Fisher OG Febechi Nwaiwu OT Nate Thomas TE Marlin Klein
The Texans are largely sitting a handful of depth pieces for this weekend on both sides of the ball. But the most notable of their inactives for this Sunday is none other than second-round rookie Marlin Klein, who will be a healthy scratch for a second straight week.
The Texans noted heading into Week 5 that they felt Brevin Jordan was a better fit on special teams than Klein at this point in the season, which led to their decision to deem him a healthy scratch this time last week.
Clearly, it seems that the same line of thinking has carried over into this week's game against Tennessee, and sets up Klein's next chance to be on the field for Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars .
The Texans also decided to sit out several other rookies brought in from this summer, albeit not as high an investment as Klein was being a second-round pick.
Fourth-round offensive lineman Febechi Nwaiwu still awaits his rookie debut as he's been inactive for the last four weeks. Seventh-round linebacker Aiden Fisher will sit out for his second healthy scratch of the season, and UDFA pickups Collin Wright and Sebastian Harsh will remain inactive this week as well.
A couple more names who will be out of the action yet don't show up on the inactives list: offensive tackle Braden Smith and wide receiver Tank Dell. Each has seen their 21-day practice window from injured reserve opened earlier this week , but the team has decided to hold off at least one more week before getting them back on the field.
S Amani Hooker TE David Martin-Robinson RB Nick Singleton RB Michael Carter CB Jaylon Jones T Brandon Crenshaw-Dickson DT Jackie Marshall
The Titans have ruled out a select few names on their side as well, with the most notable of their absences being veteran safety Amani Hooker, who had been ruled out in the days leading up to action because of a concussion he suffered in Week 4 against the Baltimore Ravens.
Tennessee has also ruled out a couple of their depth running backs for the contests as well, as rookie runner Nick Singleton and Michael Carter will be missing out. That means the Titans' backfield will be led by a three-man group of Tony Pollard, Tyjae Spears, and Julius Chestnut.
Kickoff between the Texans and Titans lands at 12 p.m. MT in Nissan Stadium, where each side is bound to be hungry to claim their first win of the 2026 season after a brutal 0-4 start.

title: How Texans’ Game vs. Titans Could Shape Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Pursuit
full_text:
Since news surfaced this weekend surrounding the Arizona Cardinals' intention to trade away wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., the Houston Texans have been largely viewed as the favorites in the mix to land him.
Rumors have connected the Texans with some of the most interest to land the Cardinals wideout, reportedly offering a future second-round pick to Arizona in hopes of landing him , and by the end of Week 5's action across the league, could have the former No. 4 pick on their roster.
But without a clear trade agreement in place for Harrison Jr. before Week 5 gets rolling, is there a chance that the Texans' matchup against the Tennessee Titans plays any role in a potential deal moving forward?
Considering where the Texans stand at this point in the season, it really wouldn't be too outlandish to say plans could shift on Harrison Jr., depending on whether they win or lose this weekend.
The situation around Harrison Jr.'s pending trade status is pretty bizarre as is: a player being inactive on gameday and on his way out in a potential deal, yet the trade package and team acquiring him are largely speculative.
Oftentimes, a player in this type of situation could've already been traded by this point in the week. But in Harrison Jr.'s case, along with what could be a pending offer on the table from the Texans, there has yet to be a clear agreement.
And this could be for a few reasons. On the Cardinals' side of things, they could simply be holding out and looking for the best package available in exchange for their former No. 4 pick.
While one team may have a second-rounder on the table, maybe another team coughs up more by the time this weekend's games end. For a premier asset like Harrison Jr., getting the best possible package will be a top priority for Arizona .
But for the Texans' side of things, there's a world where the outcome for Week 5's game against the Titans shifts their thought process of an acquisition entirely.
With a win in Nashville, the Texans can move forward as usual. They'd be 1-4, able to take a deep breath from their winless first four games, have some sense of momentum now built up, and feel a bit more confident that their second-round investment in Harrison Jr. can still be worthwhile to get wins on the board this season.
But with a loss against the Titans? The Texans then sink to 0-5. They'd find themselves in an even bigger hole than they are now, likely falling to the worst roster they've faced this season, and at a record that no team in NFL history has ever come back to make the playoffs from.
At 0-5, that win-now mindset that Houston entered the season with would be tough to continue to have. Sure, the Texans did come back from similar early-season struggles last year. But especially for the cost of a second-round pick, it makes a Harrison Jr. trade a whole lot less appealing.
So if you're a fan that wants to see Harrison Jr. in a Texans uniform by the time Week 6 rolls around, a win this weekend against Tennessee will be critical to see that dream come to fruition.
On the other hand, a loss might just leave Houston to have a major change of plans on how to move forward. So stay tuned to the results that come out of Nashville this Sunday.

title: Texans' 3 Keys to Victory vs. Titans in Pivotal Week 5 Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans have their Week 5 matchup against the Tennessee Titans right around the corner ; a game that's really a must-win for both sides as they look to escape their 0-4 record put together through four weeks.
But even while the Texans are viewed as the heavy favorites for this one, that doesn't mean this matchup will be a walk in the park.
For one, any divisional matchup can be due for some unpredictable outcomes . But we've also seen just how things can go wrong for this talented roster in the first quarter of the season for a winless start, thus giving us a blueprint on what Houston needs this weekend to ensure they get their first win on the season.
With that in mind, let's sort through three of the Texans' biggest keys to victory in Week 5 against the Titans, which could mark their seventh win in eight tries against Tennessee dating back to 2022:
The Texans finally got to see Nico Collins back in their lineup last week against the Dallas Cowboys , who returned from a two-game absence due to a hamstring strain. And in his first game back, Houston's No. 1 wideout proved exactly why he's an essential piece to their aspired offensive success.
Collins burst onto the scene with seven receptions for 118 yards and a pair of touchdowns; really for one of the best games of his entire Texans tenure, even in a losing effort. And in the process of that performance, he gave this offense a much-needed breath of fresh air.
We've witnessed how dreary this offense can be when Collins is not on the field as C.J. Stroud's top target. It's not pretty, nor is it a recipe for success. So building upon that momentum Collins saw last week feels like a good plan of attack to keep this offense from sinking as they did without him in Weeks 2 and 3.
There's no doubt about who the best player is that the Texans will be up against this weekend: it's First-Team All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, who has a chance to create some real trouble for Houston if they're not careful.
Simmons has had a similarly dominant start to his 2026 campaign, recording 24 combined tackles, three TFLs, and two sacks. And throughout the past four weeks, we've seen just what a strong interior defense can do to this Texans offensive line with the likes of Dexter Lawrence, Ed Oliver, and DeForest Buckner.
The Titans are a team that can be easily overlooked. But doing that for Simmons could be a fatal mistake for the Texans and their porous interior offensive line. So ensuring he's a center focus from start to finish will be key for Houston to keep their game script on track.
The Texans' run game has been largely the same story over the past three weeks : lacking consistency, explosiveness, and the juice needed to propel this offense to be a little more well-balanced.
Houston has failed to reach over 70 total rushing yards across the last three weeks, and their running backs have combined for less than 3.0 yards per carry across that stretch.
And without that consistency on the ground, it tends to be a major limitation for how dynamic this Texans' offense can be. That simply can't be the case moving forward this season, so maybe this outing against the Titans can be a different story.
The Titans' defense does rank top 10 in the NFL for yards per carry allowed (3.7), but they do also lead the league in carries allowed, and are 24th in total rushing yards allowed. There are holes that Houston can attack in the run game, and will likely need to in order to get the most out of their offense.

title: Texans Have 2 Other Teams to Watch in Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Talks
full_text:
The Houston Texans have found themselves as the frontrunners to watch in the ongoing trade talks surrounding Arizona Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr .
Rumors have linked the Texans to having interest in adding Harrison Jr. for a future second-round pick. Many fans and analysts, and now, even executives across the league–– according to ESPN 's Jeremy Fowler–– have circled Houston as the team who will inevitably end up landing him.
However, that's not to say they're the only ones who have generated some rumored interest in a potential move to land the Cardinals wideout––because two other teams have emerged as threats to watch as his trade saga continues to unfold over the coming days.
According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson , while there hasn't been as much noise surrounding teams with interest outside of the Texans, the trade is far from done. And until it is, the Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Chargers could be suitors to keep an eye on.
"So, this is a very, very interesting developing situation. And the trade is not done. The trade, I'm told, will not be finalized, consummated, done deal until the Cardinals finish exploring every possible trade bidder."
"Does someone else emerge? There have been some rumors about the Las Vegas Raiders, Los Angeles Chargers. We'll see. Hasn't been as much smoke. Hasn't been as much noise. Hasn't been as much concrete detail as there has been with the Houston Texans, who have not denied this trade interest."
It's a pretty unique trade situation, all things considered. While Harrison Jr. has not seen himself on the move in an official deal just yet, he's already been deemed inactive for the Cardinals’ Week 5 game against the Detroit Lions, and in all likelihood, will probably be on a new team by this time next week.
So the Cardinals have been busy shopping over the past several hours. And even with the likes of the Chargers and the Raiders seeing some connections to Harrison Jr., none of them has seen the type of chatter the Texans have throughout the past several hours–– and it makes sense.
The Texans are the only team with a reported package including a second-round pick in exchange for Harrison Jr., they have a clear need at wide receiver outside of Nico Collins, and Houston has the wide receiver's college quarterback from Ohio State in C.J. Stroud . That makes his fit in their offense even more appealing.
However, considering the talks on Harrison Jr. are ongoing––and will likely continue to be until the weekend is over–– there's certainly still a chance for the Texans to be passed up in the race to land him, if their offer ends up being beaten out by a team like the Raiders or Chargers.
Previous reports had indicated the Cardinals were in search of a second-round pick and more from the Indianapolis Colts in their previous trade talks, which led to the Colts dropping out of the race. Perhaps if another team comes out to offer that, then Arizona prioritizes their deal over whatever the Texans have in mind.
But until then, it seems like the Texans still look like the team to beat . We'll likely have more clarity on the situation once we get to the end of Sunday's Week 5 slate, but don't be shocked if it's Houston that ends up with the No. 4 pick on their roster heading into Week 6.

title: Texans Make Flurry of Roster Moves Ahead of Week 5 vs. Titans
full_text:
The Houston Texans have made a handful of roster moves on the cusp of their Week 5 matchup against the Tennessee Titans .
And no, none of those moves have involved a trade for Marvin Harrison Jr . At least, not yet.
It's a share of minor transactions for the Texans, all things considered. However, with two injured reserve activations, practice squad elevations, and even a couple of players waived, there were a few noteworthy dominoes in Houston before facing their AFC South rivals in Nashville come Sunday afternoon.
Let's break down every move the Texans made right around the corner from their Week 5 battle against the Titans:
The Texans' first of two second-round picks from this year's draft is officially good to go for his NFL debut against the Titans this weekend. McDonald had been on the injured reserve since the start of the season for an ankle injury he sustained before the year kicked off, but will now get his first chance to be a depth piece on Houston's interior behind Sheldon Rankins and Tommy Togiai.
Stewart joins back into the Texans' lineup after he had missed extended time with a quad injury sustained during the 2025 season. It's been nearly a year since we last saw the veteran safety on the field for an NFL game, but he'll make a return this weekend, likely as depth behind Reed Blankenship and as a special teams contributor.
The Texans had just signed Gronowski back to the active roster this week after he had been released back in September. Now, just a few days later, Houston will be releasing him from the 53-man roster. Gronowski will be expected to return to Houston's practice squad if he clears waivers upon his release, so this likely won't be the end of his time in the building.
The Texans added Oliver to the 53-man roster earlier this week as a depth piece in their receiver room, yet they'll be releasing him on the eve when Houston will be up against his former team in Tennessee. Like Gronowski, Oliver will also be expected to return to Houston's practice squad if he clears waivers upon his release. So barring any unforeseen changes, he'll be here to stay too.
Hall will be making his season debut for the Texans on Sunday as the team will officially be using one of his three practice squad elevations for this year. Hall was a former starting cornerback for the New York Jets before his arrival in Houston, as he's played 40 career NFL games with over 20 starts. Hall could bring some depth to the Texans' secondary unit in a pinch, but he'll most likely find his spot on the special teams side of things this weekend.
Murray is back for a second week on the Texans' 53-man roster, as he'll look to continue getting more work on Houston's defense following the 64 total snaps seen against the Dallas Cowboys. There's also a good chance Murray could find his way back into the Texans' defense as a starter this week, as he was in Week 4. Azeez Al-Shaair will be returning from his groin injury that sidelined him for a game, but Murray could uproot Jake Hansen, depending on where the coaching staff stands.

title: What Texans' Trade Offer for Marvin Harrison Jr. Might Look Like
full_text:
The Houston Texans currently find themselves as the frontrunners to trade for Arizona Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. , following some league-wide chatter surfacing just a day before Sunday's Week 5 action.
However, while the Texans might be the most frequently connected team to Harrison Jr., an official trade has yet to be announced.
One team that has had Marvin Harrison trade talks with Arizona is Houston, sources tell me and @rapsheet . Houston has been, and is thought to be, square in the mix for Harrison. But as one Texans source said about the team’s interest in Harrison, “I can’t confirm or deny at this… https://t.co/qEGc9qsJDs
The Cardinals are leaving Harrison Jr. inactive for this weekend's game against the Detroit Lions as they finalize a move for his future in the coming days, wherever that ends up being. Yet, their trade partner for him hasn't been revealed, and might not be until the weekend is over.
That next stop could very well be the Texans , depending on if the offer they've handed over to the Cardinals is deemed the best they have on the table. To this point, it's pretty hard to really say for certain.
But if the Texans were to actually be the ones making a move for Harrison Jr., what might their trade offer look like to go and get him?
At the very least, it seems like we do have some sense about what the Texans' latest offer to the Cardinals is for a potential move to acquire Harrison Jr., based on some intel from Pro Football Talk 's Mike Florio .
According to Florio, the Texans had offered a 2028 second-round pick to the Cardinals in exchange for Harrison Jr., despite Arizona pushing for an earlier pick.
"The package is expected to include a second-round pick. The Texans, we’re told, had offered a second-round pick in 2028. The Cardinals have been pushing for a second-round pick in 2027," Florio reports.
If true, the Texans seem to have come pretty close to the Cardinals' initial rumored asking price in exchange for their former No. 4 pick.
﻿ ESPN's Adam Schefter had recently reported that the Cardinals were searching for value equal to a first-round pick, and in talks with the Indianapolis Colts, they were hoping for a second-round pick and more in exchange for Harrison Jr.
Harrison Jr., while he hasn't performed up to his expectations through his first three years pro, certainly has the untapped potential that opposing front offices would be interested in investing an early-to-mid-round selection in.
After all, he's only 24 years old, still on his rookie contract, and has the scouting profile as someone who could be a real difference maker offensively, if in the right situation.
Clearly, whatever deal Arizona's front office might have on the table has made them confident enough to make their pass-catcher inactive for Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions.
And if the buzzing rumors are a sign of anything, it might just be an offer from Nick Caserio and the Texans.
In the event the Texans offered a 2028 second-rounder in exchange for Harrison Jr., they'd still have more than enough future draft capital to work with moving forward–– simply because of how conservative they've been in trading away day one and two selections.
From 2027 to 2029, the Texans possess each of their own picks from rounds one to four. Houston only has seven day three picks through that same span, yet it certainly gives this front office flexibility to go out and make a splash move like this one.
Especially for a team in the Texans' situation––looking to win now yet looking to escape their current 0-4 record––they can afford to spend their future draft capital in hopes of sparking this roster with another layer of talent, especially at a position of need like wide receiver.
Time will tell if they'll be the ones to pull the trigger. But by reading the tea leaves, it wouldn't be too hard to imagine the 2023 No. 4 pick wearing a Texans uniform by the time we get to Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars .

title: Texans Emerging as Marvin Harrison Jr. Suitor in Bizarre Trade Saga
full_text:
The NFL world was hit with a bombshell a day before Sunday's Week 5 action that made it clear that Arizona Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. was on the move to a new team via trade––yet without a clear indication of where his next home might be.
However, it looks like the Houston Texans are one of the few rumored teams with eyes on a potential trade to land the former No. 4 pick.
According to Adam Schefter of ESPN , Houston "has been, and is thought to be, square in the mix" for a trade to land Harrison Jr. as the Cardinals have been weighing their options of a move for weeks now.
One team that has had Marvin Harrison trade talks with Arizona is Houston, sources tell me and @rapsheet . Houston has been, and is thought to be, square in the mix for Harrison. But as one Texans source said about the team’s interest in Harrison, “I can’t confirm or deny at this… https://t.co/qEGc9qsJDs
Now, it's not an exact confirmation that the Texans have a package lined up for Harrison Jr. to execute at this moment––largely because an official trade for Harrison Jr. has yet to be reported on. The Cardinals simply know their time with their 2023 first-round pick is over, and are on the hunt for his new home.
Whether that trade for Harrison Jr. is already completed behind the scenes, if the Cardinals are simply searching for better offers that could beat the one they have on the table, or if the Texans are even involved is really a mystery at this point.
However, what we do know for certain is that the Texans, at the very least, have an interest in adding Harrison Jr. to their offensive arsenal. And if a move does come to fruition, it could have major implications for Houston and their scoring attack.
There are a couple of easy dots to connect as to why the Texans would be among the teams interested in striking on a talent like Harrison Jr.; someone that many considered an elite receiver prospect entering the league in 2023, yet has not seen his breakout come to fruition as expected.
For one, the Texans' wide receiver unit outside of Nico Collins has been pretty uninspiring through the first four weeks of the season.
2025 third-round pick Jaylin Noel has looked explosive in limited opportunities, and both Kayshon Boutte and Xavier Hutchinson have been worthwhile depth pieces . But none have emerged as a true No. 2 opposite of Collins. That role was supposed to be due for Jayden Higgins entering the year, but he saw his season end before it even started due to an ACL tear in training camp.
So for this Texans' receiving corps to really be at its best for the 2026 season and support C.J. Stroud with the best supporting cast possible, a trade for a starting-caliber wide receiver to line up opposite Collins could be a worthwhile investment.
And who better to bring that skillset than Stroud's former college teammate from Ohio State?
Stroud was teammates with Harrison Jr. for two seasons, where the pair really saw their connection spark during their 2022 campaign. Harrison Jr. logged over 70 receptions, 1,200 yards, and 14 touchdowns, while Stroud would find his way to becoming the Big Ten Offensive Player of the Year, and eventually, the No. 2 pick in the NFL Draft.
So when combining a receiver-needy Texans offense with talent like Harrison Jr. who's desperately in need of a change of scenery, and already has previous chemistry with Stroud, a move like this adds up pretty quickly for Houston's front office to act on.
The big question, though, remains whether or not the Texans actually have the package in place to acquire Harrison Jr.
While they are heavily rumored in the sweepstakes to land him, such a bizarre fallout of the trade hasn't given us any clear expectation of what to expect for the wideout's immediate future.
The Cardinals had been rumored to be asking for a second-round pick and more for Harrison Jr., but it remains to be seen if the Texans were among those willing to send over such a deal, or if another team emerges from the shadows to offer even more.

title: Texans-Titans Week 5 Injury Report: Updates on Tank Dell, Azeez Al-Shaair
full_text:

And for both sides, things are looking relatively clean. That's especially so for the Texans, considering they've only officially ruled out one player heading into this weekend's divisional matchup in Nashville.
Let's sort through the latest on the injury front for both sides heading into Week 5, and what it might mean for a defining matchup between two 0-4 teams in the AFC South :
WR Tank Dell: OUT (knee) S M.J. Stewart: QUESTIONABLE (quad) OT Blake Fisher: QUESTIONABLE (illness) OT Braden Smith: QUESTIONABLE (foot) OG Ed Ingram: QUESTIONABLE (illness) OT Aireontae Ersery: QUESTIONABLE (illness) DT Kayden McDonald: QUESTIONABLE (ankle)
The only name the Texans have ruled out days ahead of Sunday's matchup is wide receiver Tank Dell. It was the largely outcome to be expected for Houston's fan favorite pass-catcher for Week 5, who's gradually been returning from his severe knee injury that's left him sidelined since December 2024.
Dell's status seems to be progressing pretty well since the Texans activated his 21-day window to return from injured reserve earlier this week. He was a limited participant in practice on both Wednesday and Thursday, yet was left as a DNP for their third session.
So Dell will be out for Week 5, but will be worth watching over the next couple of weeks. He could be activated from the IR at any time between now and Wednesday of Houston's Week 8 bye.
Another piece of good news for the Texans: their starting middle linebacker and green-dot signal caller Azeez Al-Shaair was completely removed from the injury report, and is officially good to go for this weekend.
The Pro Bowl linebacker missed last weekend against the Dallas Cowboys with a groin injury he suffered the week prior, but his full participation at practice on Friday was the last domino that needed to fall before he'd been deemed active for Week 5.
That means for Al-Shaair, he'll be slotting back into his regular starting slot in the middle of the field as Houston's top linebacker, and will start next to either Jake Hansen or Kenneth Murray.
Outside of the two big names that the Texans saw take a step forward in this week's practice, Houston has listed six players as questionable for this weekend.
Three offensive linemen contracted a new illness as of Thursday's practice, which left them as DNP, but all of Blake Fisher, Ed Ingram, and Aireontae Ersery were back to participating on Friday. All three should be expected to play.
Then Houston has three returnees from IR that could make their season debut this weekend: safety M.J. Stewart, offensive tackle Braden Smith, and rookie defensive tackle Kayden McDonald . All three appear to be trending in a good direction, and could all inevitably be activated for Sunday, barring any surprises.
S Amani Hooker: OUT (concussion) TE David Martin Robinson: QUESTIONABLE (hamstring) WR Carnell Tate: QUESTIONABLE (back) CB Joshua Williams: QUESTIONABLE (pec)

Kickoff between the Texans and Titans lands on 12 p.m. MT in Nissan Stadium, where one team will inevitably check off their long-awaited first win of the season by the end of the action.

Washington has also cleared this line in two head-to-head matchups against Indianapolis. That is a matchup I expect Rodgers to take advantage of.

It's the same concern with Indianapolis' linebacker situation. With Carlies out and inexperienced players potentially stepping into bigger roles, covering Warren out of the backfield could become a major problem.
The approach is straightforward this week. Pittsburgh's run defense could force Indianapolis to lean heavily on the passing game, creating opportunities for Daniel Jones and Josh Downs to produce.
And if the Steelers manage to stall a few drives, Spencer Shrader should be right there to capitalize.
We've had success trusting the numbers on Colts props all season, and I don't see a reason to change that approach now.
