title: Patriots RB Rhamondre Stevenson Gives Positive Update on Playing Status
full_text:
FOXBORO — Late in the New England Patriots' 29-26 win over the Buffalo Bills, Rhamondre Stevenson got banged up and would exit the game on the final drive. Stevenson would be a limited participant throughout practice the week following, another injury the Patriots wouldn't be able to afford.
So as the team looks ahead to the challenge of the Las Vegas Raiders, Stevenson gave reporters a positive update for if he'll suit up or not.
"Feeling great. Ready to go," Stevenson told reporters in front of his locker on Friday. "I just got rolled up on. It was really just a little scare I had. Just really making sure I was good, honestly."
The Patriots officially listed Stevenson as questionable with a knee injury, one of seven players to enter the game with a questionable designation. But Stevenson has his sights set on playing. He's been solid — not mind-blowing — four games into the season (44 carries, 163 yards, one touchdown), but his hard running style helps set up the rest of the Patriots offense looking to stack positive weeks together.
"I've just been recovering during days like (where I'm limited). Got on the field, I ran," he said. "Ran around yesterday, and I was full go today, so I'm feeling good."
Mike Vrabel didn't rule out the possibility of Stevenson playing against the Raiders — "Not out yet. Not out as of yet," the head coach said at his weekly Friday availability.
Stevenson says that there's a heavy emphasis every week on the run game, but this week can be critical considering some of the injuries to the wide receiver room. Mack Hollins was ruled out with a calf injury he suffered in Week 4.
But it's a tough challenge against a Raiders front that includes both edge rusher Maxx Crosby and linebacker Nakobe Dean.
"Staying on the field as long as we can, keeping our defense off the field, staying ahead of the sticks," Stevenson said. "That's gonna be key."
If Stevenson wouldn't be able to go, that will mean a larger dose of snaps for TreVeyon Henderson and Corey Kiner (with a potential practice squad elevation for Lan Larison, who was elevated back in Week 1). And while nothing is set in stone just yet, it feels like it's safe to assume Stevenson will remain in the starting lineup.
"Obviously we haven't arrived yet, still a ton of work to be done," Stevenson admitted. "But I think we've progressed a little bit in that area last week out there."

title: Patriots Promote Veteran Safety Who 'Loves' Special Teams Role
full_text:
FOXBORO — The New England Patriots entered this week with a pair of open roster spots . One of those was filled up when the team promoted safety Mike Brown from the practice squad to the 53-man roster.
Brown, who was a game day elevation for each of the last two weeks , signed with the Patriots as a free agent this offseason. In the two games that he's played in this season , he's recorded 12 defensive snaps and 42 special teams snaps. Brown has two tackles this season.
Earlier in the spring, Brown was repping as the team's third safety. He then fell down the depth chart a bit, but latched onto special teams. He was released during roster cuts in August, but rejoined the team with the practice squad.
Now, he'll be given a larger opportunity to show why the team signed him to a one-year deal.
"When you think about football, you can never be where you want to be," Brown told Patriots On SI. "I'm thankful. It's part of the journey, and I'm happy to be a part of the roster now."
Brown's promotion comes after a wave of injuries hit the Patriots secondary . Christian Gonzalez, Carlton Davis, Channing Canada and Karon Prunty were all ruled out for this week's game against the Las Vegas Raiders. Charles Woods was spotted on the injury report with a shoulder injury, and the Patriots lost special teams ace Dell Pettus to an ankle injury earlier in the year.
There's a lot of moving pieces for the Patriots this week, but adding Brown to a more solidified role on the active roster should help some of the bleeding. He'll likely join Brenden Schooler, who Mike Vrabel said is ready to make his season debut after starting the year on the non-football injury list.
"He's a core special teams player, personal protector on the punt team and backup safety," Vrabel said of Brown and why the team chose to elevate him. "So, going to need him eventually."
Brown will become a regular on a special teams unit that's been solid to begin the season. It's part of his bread and butter as a player, and a part of his game that Brown takes a lot of pride in.
"I enjoy it. I mean, I wouldn't have a job without it," Brown said. "You got to embrace it. That's the way I feed my family. So I love it if it loves me."
This week will be tough for the Patriots, as they face a Raiders team who relies a lot on Brock Bowers' production. The superstar tight end has the ability to change a game, and so the Patriots' secondary will need to key in on him. Brown might not get a large dose of snaps in the defensive huddle, but all the safeties (Kevin Byard, Craig Woodson, Jaylen Reed) will be asked on to do a lot .
"Brock Bowers is unique," Brown said. "He's a big body, but he's almost like a receiver, so he can create a lot of matchup conflicts. I would say they like to run the ball, so you got to be keyed in to stopping the run and taking away the players they want to get the ball to.
"But Brock's a really good player. It's kind of weird watching him because he's so big, but he's a receiver, so it's like a very, very skilled player."

title: Saints Must Accomplish 3 Things to End Minnesota's Perfect Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (1-3) enter Sunday's Week 5 matchup against the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings (4-0) looking to bounce back from a humbling 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday night.
However, getting back on track won't be easy against a Minnesota team that has relied on one of the NFL's most dominant defenses to overcome its offensive struggles.
Sunday's matchup will also be a special occasion for the franchise as legendary quarterback Drew Brees will be inducted into the Saints Ring of Honor, adding even more significance to a game in which New Orleans desperately needs a victory.
For the Saints, the challenge will be giving their former quarterback and the home crowd something to celebrate while avoiding a third consecutive loss at the Caesars Superdome.
Doing so will require significant improvements on both sides of the ball, particularly against a Vikings defense that has consistently overwhelmed opposing offenses.
Here are three keys to victory for the Saints as they look to hand Minnesota its first loss of the season.
The Saints’ matchup against the Vikings will hinge on whether New Orleans can handle Minnesota’s league-leading blitz and pressure package. Minnesota enters Week 5 with arguably the NFL's best defense through four games, allowing a league-low 12.8 points per game while racking up 16 sacks, four interceptions and a plus-five turnover differential, the second-best mark in the league.
That is a major concern for a Saints offense that has struggled with consistency, protection, and turnovers. New Orleans has surrendered 12 sacks through four games, turned the ball over too often and enters Sunday with a minus-five turnover differential. Against a defense that thrives on disguising coverages, generating pressure from different alignments and forcing difficult decisions, the Saints cannot afford to fall behind early or repeatedly find themselves in obvious passing situations.
The biggest individual matchup is quarterback Tyler Shough against Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores ’ blitz-heavy system. Shough has already been sacked a dozen times this, with nine coming against the blitz, and New Orleans will need clear answers built into the game plan to avoid exposing him to the same issues again.
There are reasons for optimism. When Shough has gotten the ball out against blitzing defenses, he has been productive, posting a 105.1 passer rating while completing 71.9% of his passes and throwing for 442 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. But Minnesota has been uniquely effective at creating negative plays, and the Vikings’ No. 2 pressure rate will make life difficult if the Saints cannot keep the pocket clean.
Containing opposing top receivers has plagued the Saints through four games, making Sunday’s matchup against Vikings superstar Justin Jefferson a severe challenge.
Despite Minnesota ranking last in passing and 31st in total offense, Jefferson’s elite route-running, explosiveness, and contested-catch ability threaten New Orleans’ vulnerable secondary.
These defensive struggles were evident in Week 3 when Raiders tight end Brock Bowers posted 10 catches, 119 yards, and a touchdown from Kirk Cousins in Las Vegas' 31-28 win.
They continued Monday against Atlanta, as Drake London caught five passes for 96 yards, including a 37-yarder over Kool-Aid McKinstry , despite the Falcons leaning on the run.
New Orleans' secondary has struggled with missed tackles, blown coverages, penalties, and big plays.
Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. averaged 11.2 yards per attempt, going 15-for-20 for 223 yards and a touchdown.
Cornerbacks Quincy Riley (58 yards, TD allowed; 28.0 PFF grade) and McKinstry (60 yards allowed, two penalties; 29.5 PFF grade) were especially exploited.
These defensive flaws create major concerns facing Jefferson.
Unlike Bowers' versatile tight end mismatches or London's size, Jefferson combines route precision, speed, and versatility across alignments.
Leaving McKinstry or Riley isolated on Jefferson could prove disastrous for defensive coordinator Brandon Staley .
New Orleans must disguise coverages and offer safety help to force Kyler Murray elsewhere.
However, over-committing to Jefferson risks leaving tight end T.J. Hockenson (13 catches, 119 yards last week vs. Miami ) open underneath against an injured Saints linebacker corps.
Ultimately, New Orleans must force Minnesota into long, sustained drives without letting Jefferson dominate.
The four-game difference between these teams centers on protecting the football and capitalizing on errors.
Minnesota's plus-five turnover differential ranks tied for second-best in the NFL, whereas New Orleans ranks among the worst at minus-five. This 10-turnover gap clarifies how undefeated Minnesota overcomes an unproductive offense, while New Orleans loses despite averaging 367 yards and 26.3 points.
The Saints cannot afford to let turnovers, defensive breakdowns, and self-inflicted mistakes ruin offensive output against Minnesota's elite defense. Additionally, the Vikings lead the league in punt return average and rank second in kickoff return average, threatening a Saints squad already struggling with field position.
To succeed, New Orleans must secure the ball, limit penalties, convert in the red zone, force long drives, and avoid slow starts that play into Flores's pressure scheme. Even with Drew Brees honored at halftime and a supportive home crowd, emotional momentum will not offset repeated mistakes.

title: Saints DC Doesn't Hold Back in Response to Troy Aikman
full_text:
New Orleans Saints defensive coordinator Brandon Staley pushed back Thursday against criticism from ESPN analyst Troy Aikman , who said during a 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons that Staley "didn't have any answers" for Atlanta's rushing attack.
The Saints (1-3) surrendered five rushing touchdowns and 205 yards on the ground while playing without linebacker Kaden Elliss and edge rushers Carl Granderson and Anfernee Jennings . Staley acknowledged his responsibility for the outcome, but stated the comments bothered him "because they're not true."
“I did hear those comments, and I have no idea what he’s talking about.” #Saints DC Brandon Staley addresses Troy Aikman’s comments from Monday Night’s broadcast. pic.twitter.com/mukvaI6DMO
Bijan Robinson had 19 carries for 145 yards and two touchdowns while Brian Robinson had 14 carries for 62 yards and three touchdowns.
"It was a tough night for us, and certainly, I'm responsible. I'm calling the defense, but we've got a great group of guys," Staley said. "No one defended that runner last year better than us. He's a hell of a player. But our group defended him twice last year better than anyone through his time in the NFL."
Staley said he had heard Aikman's comments but had "no idea" what he was talking about as he alluded to how the Saints held Bijan Robinson to just 33 and 70 yards in both meetings last season.
With 2:43 left in the third quarter of the "Monday Night Football" broadcast, Aikman weighed in, highlighting missing personnel up front.
"Brandon Staley, he just simply doesn't have any answers. And I think he knew it when we talked to him coming in," Aikman said. "I think he knew. He didn't tell us, but the guys that are out ... their big edge rushers and guys who can play the run and set the edge, they're not on the field, and they just don't have that star defender that can erase mistakes for other people.
"This was a matchup issue coming into this game, and it's proven true."
Aikman also criticized the team's effort on Atlanta's fifth rushing touchdown and the third by Brian Robinson, noting that players were "standing around watching the play, missed tackles, just bad football."
Addressing the defensive breakdown, Staley noted that Bijan Robinson's 59-yard run on the third play was a "shock to everybody," but defended his unit's overall effort.
"There were plenty of good moments in there in the first half, but after that possession, it was really up and down," Staley said. "We did not play a good game after that fourth-down penalty. We never got our rhythm back as a defense. And that's what stood out to me. And that's why I say it was very uncharacteristic of us because, since I've been here, we've been very steady. But that game got away from us."
"Our guys have played the right way," Staley added regarding effort. "And mainly that's assignment, technique, effort, all in one. I think the other night, we were missing two out of the three. Our effort was there."
"We're focusing on Minnesota, learning the tough lessons from the other night," Staley said as the Saints prepare to host the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. "We've got the right guys to bounce back."

title: Kellen Moore and Saints Have a Serious Problem After Falcons Humiliation
full_text:
Before the season, the New Orleans Saints had high expectations after a strong finish to the 2025 season and with one of the best young quarterbacks in the league, Tyler Shough .
However, the second season of the Kellen Moore era has not gotten off to the start the organization wanted. After a 1-1 start featuring an upset win over the Baltimore Ravens in Week 2, the Saints have lost their last two games—falling in a fourth-quarter collapse to the Las Vegas Raiders and getting blown out by the Atlanta Falcons on Monday Night Football.
The loss to Atlanta has seemingly broken the dam. It was an embarrassing 45-24 loss on a night commemorating the 20th anniversary of Domecoming. TV networks, the city, the franchise and the league designated the game as a celebration of the night that rebirthed New Orleans.
Then, the Saints laid an egg in front of 73,000 fans, with former players such as Drew Brees and Steve Gleason and members of the 2006 team watching by a national audience.
What is going on with the Saints?
Slow starts remain a defining flaw of the Moore era for the Saints.
In 2025, New Orleans was outscored 122-29 in the first quarter. This minus-93 differential routinely forced the team to play from behind, despite second-half improvements after Shough took over at quarterback.
The issue persists in 2026. A Week 3 touchdown pass from Shough to Juwan Johnson against Las Vegas provided the Saints with a 6-3 first-quarter lead—their first under Moore and their first since Dec. 8, 2024, ending a 23-game drought.
However, the momentum proved brief. Against Atlanta on Monday night, New Orleans fell behind 24-7 at halftime following an early Falcons touchdown, a quick three-and-out, and a lone second-quarter score, ultimately losing 45-24.
Moore noted postgame that the team has tried various approaches to resolve the issue but has not yet found a solution.
"We have tried a number of different things," Moore said. "Obviously, we have to solve this. We have to find a way."
Dating back to 2025, the Saints continue to struggle early, leaving them constantly playing catch-up.
The Saints' secondary entered the season with legitimate questions, and four games have done little to provide answers.
New Orleans has talent on the back end, but the unit has struggled to prevent explosive plays and has compounded those mistakes with penalties, missed tackles and breakdowns at critical moments. Those issues were on full display against Atlanta, when Michael Penix Jr. needed only 20 attempts to throw for 223 yards and a touchdown. He averaged 11.2 yards per attempt and completed 75% of his passes despite Atlanta leaning heavily on its running game.
Cornerbacks Kool-Aid McKinstry and Quincy Riley had particularly difficult nights. According to Pro Football Focus (PFF) data, Riley allowed four receptions for 58 yards and a touchdown as the nearest defender, while McKinstry allowed two catches for 60 yards and committed two penalties. They finished with overall PFF grades of 28.0 and 29.5, respectively.
The problems extend well beyond one game.
Through four games, McKinstry has been targeted 22 times, allowing 13 receptions for 209 yards and one touchdown. He has surrendered four first downs while forcing four incompletions.
Riley has faced 21 targets, allowing 11 receptions for 142 yards and three touchdowns. He has allowed three first downs and forced three incompletions. The three touchdowns allowed are particularly concerning considering Riley has been targeted only 21 times.
The Saints haven't received much better production from their safeties.
Jonas Sanker has been targeted 19 times and allowed 17 receptions for 161 yards and a touchdown. He has yet to force an incompletion or allow a first down, according to PFF's charting.
Veteran Justin Reid has also struggled to consistently hold up in coverage. Opposing quarterbacks have completed 13 of 15 passes for 111 yards and a touchdown when targeting him. Like Sanker, Reid has not recorded a forced incompletion or allowed a first down through four games.
Combined, McKinstry, Riley, Sanker, Reid and Julian Blackmon have surrendered 57 receptions on 79 targets for 657 yards with seven touchdowns and only one interception. That is a 70.1% completion rate, with the five defensive backs combining for only seven forced incompletions.
If there is one defensive problem that should concern the Saints even more than their secondary, it's their inability to stop the run.
The warning signs were already there before Monday night. New Orleans entered Week 4 allowing 128.7 rushing yards per game, 27th in the NFL. Atlanta then turned that weakness into a full-blown disaster.
The Falcons rushed for 205 yards and five touchdowns on 35 carries, averaging 5.9 yards per attempt. Bijan Robinson accounted for 145 yards and two touchdowns, while Brian Robinson Jr. added 62 yards and three scores.
Worse, the Saints were overwhelmed immediately.
Bijan Robinson ripped off a 59-yard touchdown on Atlanta's third offensive play, setting the tone for an evening in which New Orleans never found an answer. The Falcons didn't need deception or a complicated offensive formula. They repeatedly attacked a defensive front that couldn't maintain its gaps or consistently finish tackles.
And this wasn't an isolated performance. New Orleans has now allowed 165, 108, 113 and 205 rushing yards through its first four games. That's 591 yards overall, an average of nearly 147.8 yards per game, which is 30th out of 32 teams in the NFL. The only two teams that have a worse rushing defense than the Saints are the Dallas Cowboys and NFC South rival Carolina Panthers .
There is a difference between losing games and losing the fanbase. Moore may be dangerously close to the latter.
Monday night's 45-24 loss to the Falcons felt like more than another defeat for a Saints team that has fallen to 1-3. New Orleans was embarrassed at home by its biggest rival on a night meant to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Domecoming, and the frustration inside the Caesars Superdome was impossible to ignore.
Fans can tolerate a rebuilding team. They can understand injuries, growing pains and a young roster making mistakes. Who Dat Nation can tolerate a close loss where the Saints fight until the final whistle, especially given the key injuries the team faced entering the game.
What becomes much harder to accept is a team consistently looking unprepared, undisciplined or incapable of matching its opponent's intensity.
That's where Moore's problem begins.
Moore was hired to give the Saints a new direction after years of stagnation. Instead, the results are beginning to look painfully familiar.
Four games should not determine a coach's future, particularly one overseeing a roster with obvious deficiencies. But patience around Moore could disappear quickly if performances like Monday's continue, especially since everyone, from the city of New Orleans to the NFL and television networks, designated that night for New Orleans to celebrate one of the city's and franchise's greatest moments.
This loss is something that they will not forget, and given their reactions across social media , it has not been pretty.
Saints fans aren't simply asking for wins right now. They're looking for evidence that the franchise is actually headed somewhere.
Against Atlanta, they didn't get much of it.

title: What Kellen Moore, Saints Players Said After Embarrassing Loss to Falcons
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints gave the city little reason to celebrate after their crushing 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Monday evening.
On a night commemorating the 20th anniversary of the Domecoming , Atlanta spoiled the occasion by jumping on New Orleans early and never relinquishing control. The Falcons rushed for 205 yards, produced several explosive plays and sent the Saints to 1-3.
Afterward, head coach Kellen Moore and several Saints players addressed the slow start, defensive breakdowns, turnovers and the disappointment of falling flat on such a meaningful night.
On his opening thoughts after the loss:
“Really disappointing game for us. Obviously, I thought the Dome was an incredible night, incredible energy. We obviously did a poor job just preparing our football team. We really, in all three phases, did not do enough to win this game. Atlanta came in and played a lot better than us.
“I didn't coach well enough, play well enough, so obviously, it wasn't good enough. We're at where we're at. We're a 1-3 football team with some good moments, but not enough consistent football to be where we ultimately want to be. We have a lot of work to do. There's a path for us, but it's going to take a lot of work to get there. We've got to keep going.”
On the Saints' continued slow starts:
“It is just disappointing. Obviously, not coaching it well enough, not executing well enough. They came out, went right down the field and scored. We went three-and-out and didn't score until the second quarter.”
On whether the Saints have tried changing things to start faster:
“We have tried a number of different things. Obviously, we have to solve this. We have to find a way.”
On the team's preparation:
“I just think, at the end of the day, they executed better than us. They played faster than us. They, obviously, ran the ball really well, created some explosive plays in the pass game. On our side of it, we weren't able to run the ball well enough. We turned the ball over, and that's a challenging formula.”
On the struggles running the football:
“We weren't able to run well, and we weren't able to put ourselves in position to have the opportunities to continue to run it and find that ability to finally get it going. When you fall behind, you play in some different circumstances. Obviously, you are going to have to adjust the plan.”
On the significance of the Domecoming game:
“We talked about it at the beginning of the week. The guys were fired up. I thought there was good energy. We just didn't execute well enough in the beginning, and they got going.”
On whether preparation was an issue:
“I don't think there's a lack of preparation. I think there's a lack of execution on some of it. We were prepared. I think the turnover early killed us, and we've got to be able to put some of those early drives together and score more points early on to get it going.
“As an offense, we knew exactly what went wrong and what went right. We just have to clean up those little things and take responsibility for that. I have to be able to put us in the right position to go out and do that. There's a lot to learn from. It obviously sucks, but we're going to keep going.”
On his left hand getting hit in the first quarter:
“Yeah, I took a helmet or something to it. I think it was just bruised up, so it should be good. I was able to play the rest of the game.”
On whether the injury affected his grip or throwing:
“No. It was just part of it. It didn't affect my right hand, obviously, so it was just something to deal with.”
On the disappointment considering the significance of the game:
“It is extremely disappointing. It is embarrassing. You can't say enough good things about the fans showing up and the entire process, what this game meant, and we fell short as a team to not get that win. That was our mission. That was my message, and we did not win.
“It was a team loss. We've got to do better on all fronts. As an offense, we have to start faster when we are going against another really good offense and be able to do our part. We've got to do a lot better there, and it starts with myself.”
On the mood in the locker room:
“Disappointed. More than anything, you lose to the Falcons like that, especially on a Monday night game, and it sucks. You can't say, ‘Oh, man that doesn't suck.’ It definitely does.
“But I do know as a team that we're extremely close and that we're going to keep going and keep our eyes forward. We have really good leadership, and our leadership admits that we've got to get better. We have to get better, watch the film and evaluate that. There's no hiding that.
“But at the same time, it is a long season, and there are a lot of games yet to be played where we can do that. There's nothing set in stone. We know that, and that's the best part about this business is that we're going to keep climbing.”
On the disappointment of the loss:
“I hate that we had a slow start. We got punched in the mouth early and look at the response. It's one of those games where we weren't good on offense, defense or special teams. You look at the second half and are ready to fight back.
“When you play a division rival it's like playing two games. When you have the Falcons coming into our building, you have to be ready. They had an early score with Bijan [Robinson]. At that point with 60 yards on the ground, we have to figure something out.
“They had almost 200 yards rushing (205). That's on the defensive line. When you have a ground game like that, then you have to tell the defensive line to tighten up. Our secondary had to come down and try to focus on the run and then that's when they have their way. They had their way tonight. It's embarrassing.”
On why the Saints couldn't stop Atlanta's rushing attack:
“Without sounding redundant. A 60-yard (59) touchdown. We didn't shut down our run defense. Our run defense did not show up to play early on. A 60-yard touchdown.
“From there, they see that their zone schemes are working, so they relied on that. For whatever reason, we couldn't tighten up our gaps. Our gap integrity has to be at a premium, especially when you have a top-tier back like Bijan or any running back the way that we were playing. It just wasn't good enough.”
On what the Saints should expect moving forward:
“Football is not always what you expect it to be. It is a good thing that we have 17 weeks. We have to stay encouraged. We have to have the mindset that this is not a defining moment.
“We can't take a step back because the rear view mirror is smaller than the front mirror. So, let's just keep it there.”
On whether someone needs to speak up after the loss:
“Nobody has to speak for it. Nobody says we have to step it up. Everyone knows that. Go make plays. Make this happen. We start with turnovers. We start with shooting ourselves in the foot. It's all obvious.
“We know that and we all have to be intentional about it. We play smarter ball and the results are different. These are all things that we can control. The outcome will be the outcome. We just have to control what we control and let the results speak for themselves.”
On whether Atlanta's play-action game surprised the Saints:
“We weren't surprised. We feel like we knew what they were going to do, but we just have to be better. Keep your eyes open and be ready to defend anything that you are going to get.”
On what hurt the Saints defensively:
“No, we just feel like we didn't play our best game and they played one of their best games. Congrats to them.”
On whether Atlanta's running game opened everything else up:
“I mean, we know that they are going to get some runs off. We just have to be better all across the board including the run game and pass game.”
On the offense's performance:
“There are a lot of things that we have to fix. We started out slow. We talk about starting fast and we didn't do that. We lost the ball as well. There are a lot of things here and there.
“There was a lot of emotions this game. Obviously, it was a tough…

title: Saints Humiliated by Rival Falcons in 45-24 Monday Night Rout
full_text:
In what was supposed to be a night of celebration for New Orleans and its resilience following Hurricane Katrina, with the game designated as the 20th anniversary of the Domecoming, the Atlanta Falcons made it a night of dread.
The Falcons defeated the New Orleans Saints 45-24, and it was not close from start to finish as the Falcons led the entire way . The Falcons outgained the Saints 410-320, but the margins really separated them in yards per play. Atlanta averaged 7.5 yards per play while New Orleans averaged 4.6.
While Atlanta quarterback Michael Penix threw efficiently, completing 15 of 20 passes for 220 yards and a touchdown, its rushing attack killed the Saints.
The Falcons rushed for 205 yards after Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson ran roughshod over the Saints’ depleted defense.
Bijan Robinson had 19 carries for 145 yards and two touchdowns, while Brian Robinson had 14 carries for 62 yards and three touchdowns.
Tyler Shough did have a decent game, completing 30 of 48 passes for 288 yards and a touchdown. Chris Olave had a quiet but productive day, catching 8 for 114 yards, but it was overshadowed by the beatdown the Falcons put on the Saints.
Tyler Shough did have a decent game, completing 30 of 48 passes for 288 yards and a touchdown. Chris Olave had a quiet but productive day, catching 8 for 114 yards, but it was overshadowed by the beatdown the Falcons put on the Saints.
Otherwise, the Saints had no bright spots offensively, rushing the ball 15 times for 50 yards, an average of 2.6 yards per carry. Meanwhile, Atlanta averaged nearly 6 yards per carry.
The first half was another slow start for the Saints as they trailed 24-7 at halftime.
The Falcons had the ball on the first possession and needed only three plays to score.
After Penix found Drake London and tight end Austin Hooper for gains of 12 and 9 yards, Bijan Robinson got the handoff, bounced to the outside and proceeded to go 59 yards to the house untouched to take an early 7-0 lead with 13:43 left in the first quarter.
On its second drive, New Orleans looked as if it were finally going to get something going offensively. However, a third-down stop by Atlanta led to a 52-yard field goal attempt by Daniel Carlson that he hooked to the left.
Luckily, the Saints’ defense made up for it with a quick three-and-out. Then disaster struck.
Saints running back Kendre Miller coughed up the ball on the first play and the Falcons recovered it. Miller was originally ruled down before an official review reversed the decision.
A few plays later, Bijan Robinson scored his second touchdown rush of the game to give Atlanta a 14-0 lead with 52 seconds left in the first quarter.
The Saints responded quickly as Shough unloaded a 44-yard pass to Olave that put the Saints on the 10-yard line. Two plays later, Alvin Kamara scored his first rushing touchdown of the season from 3 yards out to cut Atlanta’s lead to seven points.
That’s where the fun stopped.
Atlanta scored on the ensuing possession as Brian Robinson reached paydirt on a 4-yard touchdown run to finish off a 10-play, 65-yard drive to take a 21-7 lead.
The Falcons scored the final points of the half on a 29-yard field goal from Nick Folk .
The Saints entered the second half needing something close to a complete reversal after Atlanta built a 24-7 halftime lead. Instead, the Falcons continued to control the game and never allowed New Orleans to seriously threaten their advantage.
New Orleans opened the third quarter with one of its better sustained drives of the night. Tyler Shough moved the offense downfield with completions to Olave, Juwan Johnson and Kamara, but the Saints stalled before reaching the end zone and settled for a Carlson field goal to cut Atlanta's lead to 24-10.
Atlanta immediately answered.
Penix connected with Jahan Dotson for a chunk gain before Bijan Robinson continued to punish the Saints on the ground. London later moved the chains through the air, and Brian Robinson Jr. finished the possession with his second rushing touchdown of the night, stretching Atlanta's advantage to 31-10.
The Saints finally found the end zone again early in the fourth quarter. Shough connected with Devaughn Vele and Kamara during the drive before Kamara powered into the end zone for his second touchdown, trimming the deficit to 31-17.
Any hope of a comeback disappeared almost immediately.
Atlanta responded with another explosive scoring drive, highlighted by a 28-yard catch-and-run from Kyle Pitts and Penix's 31-yard touchdown pass to Dotson. After the Falcons' defense stopped New Orleans on downs, Brian Robinson broke loose for his third touchdown of the game to make it 45-17.
New Orleans added a late touchdown when Shough found Vele in the back of the end zone, but by then the outcome had long been decided.
Vele finished with six catches for 54 yards
The Saints were able to move the football more effectively after halftime, but nearly every positive stretch was answered by Atlanta. The Falcons scored 21 second-half points and consistently prevented New Orleans from turning the game into a legitimate comeback, finishing off a 45-24 victory.

title: Giants vs. Commanders Live Blog: Updates, Analysis and Reaction From Week 5
full_text:
The New York Giants and Washington Commanders share one of the league’s oldest rivalries, with two teams that regularly slug it out for the ‘W.’
They’ll do so again today in what is predicted to be wet and miserable weather—perfect football weather, some might say—at Northwest Stadium, home of the Commanders.
If the rain forecast holds, it will mark the second week in a row the Giants play in sloppy, wet conditions.
“I feel like we've gotten a lot of practice. Our very first camp practice was in the rain,” said head coach John Harbaugh.
“We should be fine. But we're still going to be intentional about it and focused on it. Ball handling, throwing the ball, catching the ball. And footing, too. Footing is another big deal. It's even a bigger deal on a grass field like that. We're going to have to really be thinking about our footing.”
They better be thinking about that and more because the Giants are up for a chance to keep a hold on sole possession of first place in the division and to take a 2-0 lead over their division opponents.
“Yeah, I think you take notice. It's talked about, probably not too specifically,” said Harbaugh when asked if he pays attention to what’s going on in the division at this point.
“It's more like you talk about it probably at work with your colleagues and friends and stuff. ‘You see the game last night?’ You kind of keep track of a little bit of the division, certainly more than the other teams that you're playing against.”
The Commanders, meanwhile, are back from their 30-13 loss to the Colts in London with a banged-up football team looking to steady its ship against a divisional foe they've beaten in the last four meetings, two by one score or less.
But in some good news for the Commanders, they will have Jayden Daniels, their starting quarterback, back in the lineup after a two-week absence due to a left elbow injury that will now require Daniels, whom head coach Dan Quinn said will have no restrictions, to wear a protective brace.
Can Daniels, who has been a nuisance to the Giants defense in the past because of his dual-threat ability, keep tormenting Big Blue? Or will the Giants offense have a huge, productive day against a struggling Commanders defense?
Follow along with our live blog, featuring a curated collection of observations, highlights, and more leading up to and through the game.
And don’t forget to check New York Giants On SI after the game for our complete postgame coverage.

title: Giants, Commanders Inactives: McLaurin Active; McCarthy Moves Up to QB2
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy is officially No. 2 on the quarterback depth chart.
McCarthy will serve as the backup quarterback behind starter Jameis Winston in this week’s game against the Washington Commanders. Jake Haener, who was signed to the 53-man roster from the practice squad this week, will be the emergency quarterback.
McCarthy, who is on a crash course to learn the Giants’ offense, drew rave reviews from offensive coordinator Matt Nagy this week when asked how he has been progressing in learning the system.
“I would say it’s an A-plus. He’s doing really well. That’s as best as I can put it,” Nagy said. “You look back seven days ago when we were up here having the same conversation, he’s much further along, which is, again, a credit to our position coaches and (quarterbacks coach) Brian Callahan, (offensive quality control coach) Mike Snyder.
“These guys are spending a lot of time putting time in with J.J. and with Jake (Haener) just in case. At the same point in time, J.J. is spending a lot of time trying to learn everything. So, that part has been great. Proud of him, but this is just the beginning. But I’d say A-plus right now.”
Head coach John Harbaugh admitted that the team had a package of plays for McCarthy in its offensive game plan last week against the Cardinals. It’s believed that the same package, and then some, is still in place for this week’s game against the Commanders. However, whether they’ll actually roll any of those plays out largely depends on the flow of the game and how Winston does. Winston is seeking his third straight win as a starter, something he hasn’t done since 2021 with the Saints.
Speaking of Haener, he will be the emergency quarterback after being signed off the practice squad earlier this week. League rules require the emergency quarterback to be on the 53-man roster rather than a standard practice-squad elevation.
As for the Giants’ inactive list, their lone injury-related scratch is safety Jason Pinnock, who remains in the concussion protocol after getting dinged in last week’s win over Arizona. Pinnock’s absence likely means an increased role for Ar’Darius Washington on defense.

The feeling is that Antonio Williams could be the main guy in their passing game this week, with McLaurin likely to be very limited and Stefon Diggs (hamstring) already declared out.

title: Why Giants Will Beat Washington, Why They Won’t, and a Prediction
full_text:
The New York Giants have a golden opportunity to start putting space between themselves and the rest of the NFC East if they can take care of business Sunday against the Washington Commanders in what should be a rain-soaked contest.
The Giants currently sit alone atop the NFC East. They’ve already defeated Dallas once this season, back in Week 1. By defeating Washington, New York will hold its spot atop the division standings regardless of what the Eagles, who face the Jaguars in London, do this weekend.
Moreover, a win over Washington will give the Giants a 2-0 record against division opponents, which is one tiebreaker if multiple teams end up with the same win-loss record at year’s end.
The good news for the Giants is they match up fairly well against the Commanders in just about every area of the game. It also doesn’t hurt that the Giants enter this game with better overall roster health. That said, there’s no such thing as a “gimme” game. So what will it take for Big Blue to pull off the win? And what must it avoid to keep its first loss against a division opponent from happening this season?
If there were ever a perfect setting for Giants quarterback Jameis Winston and the offense to explode for 300-plus yards and 30-plus points, this week would be it.
Washington’s defense has allowed 30.5 points per game, the third most in the league through four weeks. In fact, it has surrendered 30-plus points in its last three games.
The Giants offense finally cracked 30 points last week in a 36-24 win over Arizona (note: the last six points came on cornerback Deonte Banks’ interception). If they can keep stacking those performances, they’ll have a good chance to win every week.
Getting back to the Commanders’ defensive woes, after finishing ninth in total missed tackles last season with 155, Washington’s defense currently has the  13th most through four games (32).
Speaking of exploding, Washington has also struggled with that, thanks to breakdowns in its defensive secondary. The Commanders have allowed seven big-play pass completions of 20-plus yards, which ties them for ninth in the league. Four of those big-play passes have gone for 25-plus yards.
On the ground, things have been a little bit better. Washington has allowed nine plays of 10-plus yards. But again, if the Giants offense is ever going to blow things wide open (and they have the talent to do so), this would be a really good week for it to happen.
Washington’s red-zone defense has also struggled. The Commanders currently rank 30th in red-zone defense, with opponents converting at 80 percent. The Giants were better in the red zone last week and are tied for 18th overall, converting on 54.55 percent of their red-zone attempts. It goes without saying the Giants have to win in this part of the game, too.
With the weather expected to be a mess, the Giants will likely try to grind things out behind their running game. But that unit, which has lacked explosive plays, would be squaring off against a Washington run defense currently ranked sixth in the league (93.5 yards per game).
It’s almost certain Washington will home in on stopping the run and force Winston to beat it with his arm.
If that’s its thinking, Washington is also likely hoping for the bad side of the Jameis Winston experience: the guy who makes high-risk throws and creates opportunities for the opposing defense.
Winston, to his credit, hasn’t put the ball in harm’s way much since taking over as the starting quarterback for the injured Jaxson Dart in Week 2. Per PFF, he has thrown only four turnover-worthy passes on 78 attempts, with two coming under pressure.
Also of note, Winston has been responsible for 25.9 percent of the pressures against him , fourth-highest among 30 qualifying quarterbacks who have faced pressure on at least 25 dropbacks.
If the Giants don’t keep Winston clean when he has to pass, things could get ugly quickly.
On the other side, with the anticipated return of Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels, the Giants now have to account for another potential rushing threat who, in the two games he’s played this season, has averaged 7.3 yards per rushing attempt.
Don’t be surprised if the Giants assign a spy against Daniels to help keep him contained. If they can’t, it could be a long afternoon for Big Blue.
Washington enters this week’s game as a 3.5-point favorite according to FanDuel , probably because the game is at home. It also doesn’t hurt that the Commanders are getting Daniels back, and the rain forecast could help Washington, given the strength of its run defense.
The Giants have momentum on their side, even though their last two wins have been close ones. Washington, meanwhile, is back from its London game. Still, it also has a lengthy injury list: receiver Stefon Diggs has already been ruled out, and receiver Terry McLaurin will be a game-time decision.
That said, it’s hard to shake the feeling that this game, which feels like one the Giants should win, will be another close affair with the Giants coming up short.

title: Giants vs. Commanders Week 5: Time, Channel and What to Watch
full_text:
John Harbaugh and the New York Giants have made it their motto to focus on one game at a time and worry about going “1-0” each week, as they’ve built positive momentum and boast a 3-1 record through the first quarter of the 2026 season.
For the first time this year, however, that tunnel-vision mindset will be tested by what awaits the franchise in Landover, Maryland, where the Giants travel to square off with the Washington Commanders.
In the latest installment of the historic matchup, the Giants have much more at stake than growing their commanding lead in the all-time series and earning their fourth win in five games, something the organization hasn’t done since 2022.
With a win, the Giants could shift the NFC East race, with New York potentially jumping to a 2-0 record in the division and a two-game lead in the division if the Philadelphia Eagles fall to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.
The Commanders have also been hit by considerable injuries to the core of their roster, including at quarterback, where they’ve had to overcome the loss of starter Jayden Daniels, who went down in Week 2 with a left elbow injury that appeared as though it might sideline him long term.
However, Washington received positive news when it was announced that Daniels would return to the field in full form against the Giants, with head coach Dan Quinn saying the former No. 2 pick would have no restrictions in the team’s game plans.
If he can play at full strength, Daniels is a much more talented gunslinger than the recent ones the Giants have faced during their win streak. His dual-threat athleticism fuels an RPO-heavy offense that can stretch out the opposing defense and make it harder to bring him down before he can generate big plays with his arm.
Washington comes into the matchup desperate for a home win to salvage an early collapse lacking its No. 1 option. With Daniels back under center, it has the spark it needs to compete with a Giants offense that has been inconsistent since Jameis Winston took over for the injured Jaxson Dart.
Even with their impressive start, the Giants also have their own business to settle with the Commanders, who have taken the last four meetings, including the last two by more than one score, capitalizing on the Giants’ inability to come up with clutch plays down the stretch.
Their defense has finally ended that trend over the last two weeks. Still, Harbaugh’s Giants must now turn the special focus their head coach has preached into a complete game that reminds the Commanders why they still own a dominant stranglehold in the rivalry.
More importantly, doing so would help the franchise keep challenging the majority of outsiders who wrote them off the moment Dart hobbled off the turf at SoFi Stadium with a season-ending injury and claimed they couldn’t contend for the postseason.
The men inside the locker room believe they can still achieve that goal. While they won’t let their mathematical prospects fill their heads when they take the field, it looms in the background of a key divisional game they hope to win more convincingly.
Check in with New York Giants on SI for all the pregame, in-game and postgame coverage.
This Sunday’s game marks the 189th all-time meeting between the Giants and Commanders, dating back to the 1932 season, when the latter franchise was known as the Boston Braves.
The Giants currently hold an impressive 108-75-5 advantage in the series, but things have shifted toward the Commanders over the last couple of seasons. Washington has taken six of the last 10 meetings, including the previous four dating back to the start of the 2024 season.
Last season, the Commanders took their home contest, 21-18, then traveled to MetLife Stadium in Week 15 and defeated the Giants again, 29-22, to complete the series sweep.
The Giants’ last victory over Washington came on Nov. 19, 2023, a 31-19 road win for Big Blue.
The game will be televised on FOX. Chris Myers will handle the play-by-play duties, with former NFL defensive lineman Jonathan Vilma joining him as an analyst and Megan Olivi as the sideline reporter.
Fans can listen to the radio broadcast on WFAN 101.9 FM. Bob Papa will be the play-by-play announcer, with Giants legends Car Banks and Howard Cross joining him as the analyst and sideline reporter.
Clete Blakeman will be the head official for Sunday's contest. Blakeman joined the NFL in the 2008 season, when he started as a field judge and served two years before getting the referee promotion in 2010.
The veteran official has served in nine postseason games, three conference championships and led the team that officiated Super Bowl L between the Carolina Panthers and Denver Broncos

title: NY Giants Week 5 Officiating Crew Scouting Report
full_text:
The New York Giants (3-1) played a much cleaner game in last Sunday’s 36-24 victory over the Arizona Cardinals, at least on penalties, but they should be at greater risk in a Week 5 road matchup against the Washington Commanders (1-3). The officiating crew can be flag-happy at times.
Clete Blakeman will operate as the lead referee for this NFC East collision, per FootballZebras.com, a development that should have the Giants on their best behavior.
His crew has doled out 65 penalties through four games this season, which is the fifth most, according to NFLPenalties.com. The yardage is a bit easier to swallow, coming in at 435 (eighth most). More than half of that total came in the last two weeks, though, so things are trending in an unfavorable direction.
The 17th-year ref will be joined by umpire Scott Walker, down judge Andy Warner, line judge Kent Payne, field judge Karina Tovar, side judge James Coleman, back judge Jonah Monroe, replay official Chad Adams, and replay assistant Adam Choate.
The Giants fared quite well the last time they saw Blakeman. Actually, it was the peak of their season.
Big Blue accumulated six penalties for 55 yards in a 34-17 Thursday Night Football victory over the Philadelphia Eagles on Oct. 9, 2025. Only one of those infractions went against the defense. Blakeman’s crew does have a new umpire and replay assistant, though, so you never know what could happen.
Those worried about some home-field cooking should not have much to worry about with this official. In games that Blakeman has worked this year, home teams have accrued nine more penalties and 43 more penalty yards than visiting squads.
Overall, this referee assignment is shaping up fine for Big Blue. New York already has enough on its plate without incurring the official’s wrath. It is one thing to squeak out wins at MetLife Stadium, but there will likely be less room for error in Landover, Maryland.
Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels can be a tricky opponent for a defensive line that remains spotty against the run. The onus will fall on Abdul Carter and the pass-rushing attack to exploit an unpredictable offensive line. Dennard Wilson definitely accomplished that objective last week.
As the Giants try to win these pivotal matchups, Blakeman will keep a watchful eye on the field. The opening kickoff is scheduled for 1 p.m. ET.

title: Giants Report Card: Grading Every Position Group After the First Quarter of 2026
full_text:
Grading the first quarter of the 2026 New York Giants season is tricky because early exams featured questions neither team nor fan base expected to answer.
Quarterback Jaxson Dart and outside linebacker Brian Burns suffered season-ending knee injuries, forcing both the offense and defense to adjust their game plans. Big Blue is developing an identity regardless, showing just how much a competent head coach can fix. Today, though, we’ll focus on the players.
Let’s take a deeper dive into New York’s position groups and try to put a mark on their overall performance so far. It’s report card time!
Dart’s superb outing against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 1 keeps this grade from dropping even further. Despite making some winning throws versus the Arizona Cardinals, Jameis Winston has been largely unreliable while filling in at quarterback.
The first overall pick in the 2015 NFL Draft has completed just 55.1 percent of his passes for 479 yards and two touchdowns, while also tossing three interceptions. His usually strong arm looked absolutely shot in his first two outings, but he displayed his signature deep-ball magic last Sunday.
And his signature deep-ball unpredictability. That is the “Famous Jameis” fans know and tolerate.
If the good outweighs the bad , as it arguably did against Arizona, then New York’s offense may be able to stay afloat. But if he reverts to his September form, then J.J. McCarthy will be taking snaps under center.
The Giants’ backfield hasn’t been pretty aesthetically or efficiently, but Cam Skattebo and Najee Harris are executing John Harbaugh’s blueprint quite nicely.
The running back duo is wearing down defenses with their physical running style, helping the offense control the clock. Skattebo is averaging only 3.5 yards per carry, but that number should rise as he moves further away from last year’s gruesome ankle injury . The 28-year-old Harris is averaging 4.0 yards per rush while showing plenty of power.
Tyrone Tracy Jr. could potentially provide valuable explosiveness, just as he did on his 55-yard kick return versus the Cardinals. Still, Harbaugh clearly does not want him logging carries, at least not right now.
Despite posting a combined 46 receiving yards in Weeks 2 and 3, Isaiah Likely has been a welcome addition to the Giants offense. He thrived in the season opener, catching all eight of his targets for 78 yards and two touchdowns. The veteran tight end added another 66 yards against Arizona. He is the reliable No. 2 target fans were hoping for.
Theo Johnson is a fine backup option. The inconsistent but physically gifted pass-catcher made a strong touchdown catch to give the Giants the lead for good in last Sunday’s win. He remains a viable red-zone threat.
I don’t want to overly penalize the Giants’ wide receiver group for Winston’s shortcomings, but there’s plenty of room for improvement.
Malik Nabers enjoyed a productive NFL return against the Cowboys, and he looked like his old self in a Week 4 meeting with the Cardinals. The 23-year-old was simply electric, leaping up to make terrific grabs and exhibiting impressive bursts.
If he builds momentum, this grade should rise noticeably by season’s end. Other than Nabers, no wideout has 10 catches. Rookie Malachi Fields has shown promise, though (15.8 yards per reception), and Darnell Mooney has a couple of key first downs.
This squad’s passing attack may be limited for the remainder of the campaign, so New York will need to define itself in the trenches.
I was rather lenient with the backfield earlier, partly because the interior O-Line can help Skattebo and Harris much more. Francis Mauigoa is finding his way at right guard, and Jon Runyan Jr. has been playing better after a rough first couple of games, but John Michael Schmitz remains a weak link at center.
Bryan Hudson did not give up a sack or pressure on Sunday, so if Harbaugh makes a switch, the unit could collectively improve.
Penalties are also an issue. Runyan and Jermaine Eluemunor have combined for nine through the first four games.
This O-Line has top-10 potential, especially with Eluemunor and Andrew Thomas protecting the outside. But the Giants might need a couple of tweaks and more discipline to meet that standard.
The Giants gained traction as a dark-horse playoff pick in the preseason, but one of the main reasons many people remained skeptical was this specific position group. With Dexter Lawrence gone, it was hard to tell how ineffective Big Blue’s defensive tackle unit would be in 2026.
The results have been pleasantly surprising. Although D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris boast a wealth of experience and have been mostly reliable throughout their respective NFL careers, it was fair to wonder if the team was asking too much of them.
That could still be the case, but Reader has been an especially active presence on the defensive line. He has four stops and four total pressures this season, doing his part to patch up the Giants’ leaky run defense.
Harris has been far more volatile, but he can obviously still impact a game. The 35-year-old got his hands on a Jacoby Brissett pass and enabled rookie Arvell Reese to record a pivotal interception in Week 4. Additionally, he has no missed tackles in 118 defensive snaps .
This tandem has done a fine job of minimizing the damage left behind from Lawrence’s departure. That being said, the Giants are still allowing opponents to rush for 4.7 yards per attempt .
Even before Burns tore his ACL , New York’s pass rushers were not close to their collective ceiling. Generating sufficient pressure should be extremely difficult now, but Abdul Carter is still lurking on the edge.
The 22-year-old outside linebacker bounced back after quiet showings versus the Los Angeles Rams and Tennessee Titans, and he ravaged the Cardinals’ O-Line. His low sack total has to improve, but he is still a game-changer.
Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson will have to cover the Burns-sized hole and give Carter more chances to feast.
Excluding an awful night in Los Angeles against the Rams, the Giants’ revamped linebacker unit has carried itself quite well so far.
Reese was a human wrecking ball against Arizona, moving across the field to make one positive play after another. He boasts an NFL-leading 27 solo tackles and also has four passes defended. Dynamic and productive, what more can fans want from a No. 5 overall draft pick?
They could ask a bit more from Tremaine Edmunds, however. The two-time Pro Bowler is in the first season of a three-year, $36 million contract. Even so, he is still a solid tackler and versatile defender. A previous area of weakness is becoming a strength.
Tyler Nubin has had tough moments ( 19.3 yards allowed per reception ), but Jevon Holland’s early-season brilliance gives the safety room a well-deserved A.
The former Miami Dolphins defensive back amassed a career-high three interceptions in the first three games of the campaign, including a game-sealing one in the end zone against Tennessee. Secondary specialist Wilson is expertly accentuating his playmaking abilities .
Holland has also recorded two forced fumbles, one fumble recovery and four passes defended. He is arguably the Giants’ MVP through Week 4.
We will call this a rising C after Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome II helped the team earn its third win of the season. The former clinched it with a pick-six and played excellent coverage overall, while the latter prevented some big gains. The cornerback room is still a work in progress, though.
The Giants gave Paulson Adebo $38.5 million guaranteed to top the depth chart, but he has been both unreliable and unhealthy. Rookie second-rounder Colton Hood is promising yet raw, so Banks and Newsome will have to shoulder the workload this season.
While the results may look more mixed against superior competition, this duo is inspiring optimism that did not exist before September.
Both sides of the ball have shown more physicality and athleticism, but the biggest change…

title: 3 Matchups That Will Decide Giants' Week 5 Game Against Commanders
full_text:
The first quarter of the New York Giants season has no doubt been a rollercoaster stretch, one that saw them pick up two unbelievably gritty victories after game-ending turnovers forced by the defense, putting the franchise at 3-1 atop the NFC East.
Entering Week 5, the Giants return to a battle with the division, and possibly their toughest matchup since Week 2 against the Rams, when they visit the Washington Commanders for the first time this season in a game that suddenly holds major significance for both parties.
If the Giants can trounce the Commanders and add another tally to both their win column and division record, the whole narrative surrounding the rest of their campaign, which once looked lost without Jaxson Dart, could vastly change as the team vies for a postseason berth.
Before they can look too far ahead, Big Blue must gain the upper hand in these three matchups that will likely determine their fate against the Commanders.
After a few games on the shelf with an elbow injury, Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels has been cleared and will return to the huddle against the Giants.
Daniels suffered a dislocated elbow in Week 2 against the Dallas Cowboys, the same one he injured in Week 14 last season, which caused him to miss the final four games, including the second meeting with New York, which Washington won 29-21 to sweep the annual series.
The former No. 2 pick will have to wear a brace to protect his compromised arm. Still, he fully participated in the team’s practices leading into Sunday and is unlikely to have any limitations on his game as they aim to challenge the Giants’ defense with his dual-threat abilities and steal a much-needed win to stay in the division race.
Beyond what sets him apart from the other quarterbacks they’ve faced, Daniels has moved the football successfully against the Giants’ defense. In three games against them, he has completed 70.4 percent of his pass attempts for an average of 222.7 yards per contest with three touchdowns.
While Quinn said the game plan will not contain his quarterback, it’s fair to wonder how much Daniels will be willing to put his body on the line in a Washington offense that lives heavily on RPOs and extending plays with his legs.
Daniels will certainly benefit from solid protection from his offensive line, which enters Week 5 as the No. 3 unit in pass-block win rate . However, the Giants defense should still look to send a heavy dose of pressure in the opposing quarterback’s direction to test his confidence.
Moreover, it would be interesting to see if Dennard Wilson elects to use Carter as a spy on Daniels. Carter has the speed and instincts to follow the quarterback and burst through a gap to create some pressure if he tries to spill out of the pocket and escape for yardage.
Carter stepped up big last week against the Cardinals, notching a season-high six pressures, including three hits and two run stops, to help the Giants fluster Jacoby Brissett and the Arizona offense that tried to attack the vulnerable secondary in search of a game-winning score.
He could again be key in two ways against the Commanders: keeping Daniels from killing the Giants with his legs and forcing errant throws as he tries to protect his body from pain in that elbow.
One of Nabers’ favorite matchups since entering the NFL in 2024 has been the Washington Commanders, and the Giants receiver will have a chance to build on his breakout game against the Cardinals in Week 4 as he faces their weaker secondary again on Sunday.
Nabers has been active in three meetings between the two rival franchises, where he has been a top target against a unit that struggles to keep the ball out of his hands. He has collected 24 catches for 257 yards and one touchdown against Washington and been targeted at least 11 times in each contest.
The LSU product got off to a hot start in the NFC East series as a rookie, when he caught 10 of 18 targets for 127 yards and the lone score, but his stellar outing was marred by a late drop in the fourth quarter that stalled the Giants’ attempt to score a go-ahead touchdown and led to a 21-18 loss.
Since then, his impact on the division rivalry has not led to a victory for New York. That’s a reality Nabers wants to change, especially given his college ties to Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels and the bragging rights that come with their relationship.
The good news for Nabers is the Commanders have not been a fearsome coverage team so far this season. Washington ranks 25th or worse in passing yards, touchdowns, and average yards per attempt, as their starting options (Amik Robertson, Rasul Douglas, and Fabian Moreau) have been picked apart, posting an average 72.5 percent completion percentage for 279 yards.
Moreau, a former Giant, jumped into the starting right-side cornerback role amid third-year teammate Mike Sainristil’s struggles, but has been active for only two games and is a fairly new piece in the Commanders’ defensive scheme who will likely see a lot of one-on-one matchups with Nabers.
The Giants should look to attack that matchup in volume and turn Nabers into their most productive weapon on Sunday. Two obstacles to a potential breakout performance are the poor conditions expected at Northwest Stadium and the Commanders’ heavy blitzing.
Washington enters Week 5 having relied on the blitz at the second-highest rate in the NFL (49.3 percent), and with Jameis Winston’s recent showings under center, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see the Commanders send the heat his way in hopes of getting him to make some poor throws.
If Nabers is going to have a big impact in Sunday’s game, he might have to do it with a lot of quick passes before the middle of the Giants’ offensive line crumbles, and Winston feels the pressure. The hope is that he can hit a few deep looks as he did against Arizona and finally get over his losing hump against the Commanders.
With the rainy conditions set to blanket the Landover area heading into Sunday, the Giants may have to call on their backfield to carry the load.
The run game has been a key component of the Giants’ offense over the last couple of games. They faced the same poor conditions against the Titans in Week 3, and the running backs room helped New York control the clock and hang onto its 12-7 win with a combined 33 rushes for 138 yards.
It was heading in the same direction last week against the Cardinals before the weather settled and John Harbaugh and company attacked the opposing secondary, with the passing game highlighted by Winston’s three touchdown passes and Nabers’ average of 18.7 yards per catch.
Now, the story could revert to two weeks ago, as the playing environment is expected to be less than forgiving to both franchises. If it does, the matchup could create a problem for the Giants’ group of ball carriers.
Led by Cam Skattebo, the Giants rank fifth in rushing attempts and 13th in yards. Their average per carry (3.7) needs to improve, but the Commanders’ front seven could stand in the way, allowing the sixth-lowest yards per contest and an average of 4.0 yards per carry to opponents in four games.
The key to their trench prowess has been strong tackling: Washington’s front has whiffed on three total tackles while making 43 run stops and averaging 2.78 yards in distance of tackle .
The Giants don’t create many explosive runs , so that weakness could get exposed against the Commanders, who want to force them into longer distances and make Winston author big-time throws amid what could be a ton of pressure.
At the same time, the Commanders haven’t faced a running back of Skattebo’s caliber. Skattebo could be the perfect guy to counter their strength in the gaps with his ferocious running style and physicality, fighting for every yard in front of him.
If Skattebo can get his motor going early and wear down Washington’s first two levels, the Giants will open up the hard-nosed style of football that has been the backbone of their offense and help…

title: Why the Giants’ Run Game Hasn’t Clicked, and What Needs to Change
full_text:
Through four weeks of the 2026 NFL season, the New York Giants have apparently tried to run a ground-and-pound offense that puts their running game at the center of the attack.
But the Giants’ running game has been sputtering along, even with a healthy Cam Skattebo back in the lineup and taking the bulk of the carries.
New York ranks 13th in the league in total rushing yardage (442), but its average of 3.7 yards per rushing attempt ranks 23rd.
“I think we haven’t fully come into our own yet,” Skattebo said this week. “I think up front, we’re in a new scheme, new system, and these guys are learning.”
Perhaps, but other than Bryan Hudson, who replaced John Michael Schmitz at center last week, the unit has worked together not only for the first four games (91 rushing attempts, seventh most in the league through three games), but also throughout the OTAs and training camp.
A deep dive into the numbers confirms that the quarterback position was a secret ingredient in the team’s 2025 rushing success, with the Giants finishing as a top-five unit that season.
Based on what the Giants running backs alone contributed to the rushing game in 2025, New York would have finished 15th in total rushing yards (1,587) and 24th in average yards per attempt (4.0), below the 4.3 average the unit posted with quarterback-position contributions.
Jumping back to the present season, the Giants have been heavily leaning on Skattebo to lead the rushing charge. Skattebo has the most carries of any Giants runner (68 attempts), with the next closest competitor being Najee Harris, who was inactive in Week 1, with 22.
Tyrone Tracy Jr., who had some ball security issues (as has Skattebo) in the preseason and earlier in the year, has all but disappeared from the rotation.
And when he has been on the field this season, the Giants’ rushing attack has been better, averaging 4.0 yards per rushing attempt versus 3.7 yards per attempt when he has not been on the field.
What about explosive runs? They’ve definitely been hard to come by for the Giants so far. New York has eight rushes of 10-plus yards (including by the quarterbacks), which ties them for 21st in the league.
They have one rush of 20-plus yards (23rd), and they are among nine teams that have not registered a 25-plus-yard rush so far in 2026.
“We definitely need more explosives in the run game. That’s definitely something that we’ll be chasing and looking for,” head coach John Harbaugh said.
“It’s really our execution mostly, usually. Sometimes you’re overwhelmed with numbers or something like that. But there’s definitely been plays where we can get more yards on.”
Skattebo, as the lead runner, agreed, adding that there are things he can do to help contribute to the overall production, hinting at potentially avoiding unnecessary contact in favor of seeking holes for more yardage.
Skattebo, per PFF, is averaging 0.68 yards before contact, 37th among NFL running backs, but 2.78 yards after contact, 28th in the league.
“I kind of like to punish my opponents. When game seven, eight, nine comes around, they’re not going to want to do that. That’s when you kind of get to run past them, when they lower their shoulder and close their eyes,” he said.
“Right now, I’m just doing me. I obviously could probably make a move here and there, but sometimes it’s better for the team, beating up on the other team,” Skattebo added.
“I’ve got to be better, obviously, in the run game. I could definitely make a couple different cuts a game and completely change the outcome. I’m going to continue to work on that and continue to grow.”

title: Biggest Area Where the Giants Need to Improve in Chase for NFC East Title
full_text:
The New York Giants have the pieces to run a pass-first offense, except for a reliable quarterback. Jameis Winston proved he can still sling the ball for big gains downfield, but he also proved he can still give the ball to the opposition at a costly rate. The former Pro Bowler cannot carry this offense.
The Giants must establish the run, and to do that, they must block more consistently for their backfield.
Cam Skattebo is averaging an inefficient 3.5 yards per carry. Najee Harris is gaining a more respectable 4.0 yards per attempt, but he has only run the ball 22 times through four games. These two power backs will need more support from their offensive line to inflict true damage.
The Giants are expertly concealing their biggest weaknesses by controlling the clock and wearing down defenses. How long can they execute that plan without sufficient protection, though?
New York has taken advantage of inferior competition this season, and that is certainly something to celebrate. The 2025 G-Men would have let the last two wins slip through their grasp. There is obvious improvement.
But if the franchise is going to hold off the Philadelphia Eagles and capture its first NFC East title since the Super Bowl-winning 2011 campaign, it will need to stay strong on the line and open lanes for its running backs.
Tackles Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor are obviously coveted for their pass-protection skills, but they are staying steady in run-blocking situations as well. The interior O-Line is the issue.
Jon Runyan Jr. has struggled to find consistency this season, and his five penalties are probably only making it harder for him to get into a groove. Fellow guard Francis “Sisi” Mauigoa is still learning the position after moving from tackle so New York can wait out his growing pains.
John Michael Schmitz is a question mark. Now in his fourth NFL season, he has missed 10 games thus far in his career and has been shaky since his rookie season.
After a sluggish start, he was replaced last week by Bryan Hudson, who made the most of his opportunity by not allowing any sacks , pressures, or hurries.
Hudson could have some tough moments, but after what he displayed in Week 4, the 25-year-old could be the key to unlocking this offensive line. More stability in the middle, coupled with the continued development of Mauigoa, should lead to better production in the running game.
Skattebo, Harris, Tyrone Tracy Jr., and Devin Singletary still have to do their part, but their success rate should significantly rise if the O-Line provides proper cover.
If they achieve this crucial objective, everything should fall into place. The Giants can set the tone on the ground, which in turn eases Winston’s burden. A sound offense can complement a rising defense, positioning New York for divisional glory.
The vision is there. Now, Big Blue must bring it to life.

title: Giants Place Chauncey Golston on IR, Elevate Two From Practice Squad
full_text:
The New York Giants have elevated wide receiver Dalen Cambre and outside linebacker Trace Ford from their practice squad and have placed defensive lineman/outside linebacker Chauncey Golston on IR.
Golston suffered a neck injury in last week’s win over the Arizona Cardinals. Before that, he missed five consecutive games in 2025 due to a neck injury. It is unknown whether what caused him to miss those games is the same issue bothering him this season.
Golston was the only Giants player who was ruled out for Sunday’s game against the Washington Commanders and did not travel with the club this week. Safety Jason Pinock, also ruled out with a concussion, is believed to have made the trip.
This week marks Cambre's first elevation, adding depth on special teams and at receiver, and Ford's second, with help on special teams and on defense.
With Golston placed on IR, the expectation is that Jihad Ward, who was signed to the 53-man roster last week off the Vikings practice squad, will be active and have a sizable role on defense by taking on Golston’s role.
The Giants also have an opening on the 53-man roster, as they did not fill Golston’s spot.
One possibility for the open spot, assuming there are no more notable injuries, is to open the 21-day practice window for cornerback Korie Back, who was placed on IR during training camp but was also designated to return.
